devotionals.title: No Longer a Slave, but a Son
devotionals.verse: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!' So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
body: "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!' So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God." — Galatians 4:4–7

Paul wrote to the Galatians — Gentile believers being lured back toward slavery by false teachers who insisted faith in Christ was not enough and they must add the law's works. Paul answers by telling their story: once they were slaves under the elemental things of the world, but at the fullness of time God sent His Son. The setting matters, because it exposes the difference between a slave's religion and a son's. The slave works to earn the master's favor; the son already has the Father's. The Galatians were being talked back into chains — and Paul calls that return to bondage a denial of what Christ purchased.

The law lands on us first. Our hearts are natural slaves. Even in Christ we creep back to the whip each morning — bargaining with God, as if yesterday's obedience earned today's acceptance and yesterday's failure could unmake it. We treat the Father like a hard master to be appeased rather than a Father to be loved, measuring our standing by our performance. That is slavery's posture, and it is the old man's native tongue.

But hear the gospel: God sent His Son so that we might *receive* adoption as sons. Notice the word "receive" — the same empty-hand grammar as justification. Adoption is not a wage; it is a gift. In Christ the slave becomes a son, and the son becomes an heir — not a hired hand with a paycheck, but a child with an inheritance. And the proof is not in your feelings but in the Spirit: God has sent the Spirit of His own Son into your heart, crying "Abba! Father!" — the same word Jesus breathed in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), now put on your lips. Because you are united to Christ, what belongs to Him belongs to you: His Father is your Father, and His inheritance is yours.

The doctrine underneath is adoption — the Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q&A 34) defines it as "an act of God's free grace, whereby we are received into the number, and have a right to all the privileges, of the sons of God." "Free grace" — it is wholly God's doing. And it is more than acquittal: justification pardons the criminal; adoption takes the pardoned one home. John Calvin taught that this is the fruit of our union with Christ: because we are one with the Son, the Father loves us with the very love He has for Christ (John 17:23). The Puritan John Owen pressed it home in his work on communion with God: the Father does not deal with you as a stranger or a servant, but as His child — loved, pitied as a father pities his children (Psalm 103:13), and disciplined only the way a father disciplines his son (Hebrews 12:5–11).

This is the day the LORD has made (Psalm 118:24), and His mercies are new this morning (Lamentations 3:22–23). Walk into it not as a slave trying to earn the Father's smile, but as a son who already has it — crying "Abba" all day long.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the slave's bookkeeping — today's attempt to earn the Father's favor or the fear of losing it, as though God were a master to be appeased. That is the old self's religion, and it always ends in pride or dread. *Put on* the son's confidence — come to the Father this morning as His child in Christ, bringing your needs freely, asking boldly, trusting the Spirit's cry in your heart. Pray as a son, not as a hired hand.

**Prayer:** Father — my Father — thank You that You did not leave me a slave. You sent Your Son at the fullness of time to buy my freedom and make me Your child, and You sealed it by sending the Spirit of Your Son into my heart. Forgive me for crawling back to the whip, for bargaining when You have already given me everything. Teach me to cry "Abba" today — in my need, in my weakness, in my joy — and to rest as an heir. Through Jesus Christ, my elder Brother, in whose name I am bold to pray. Amen.

reflect.q: For reflection today
reflect.a: Where in your life do you still relate to God as a slave — bargaining, hiding, fearing — and what changes when you speak "Abba, Father" over it?

devotionals.title: Not My Own
devotionals.verse: For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.
body: "For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's." — Romans 14:7–8

Paul wrote these words to the believers in Rome around AD 57 — a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles, tangled in disputes over food and holy days. The arguments were real, but Paul refused to referee opinions as if they were the main thing. He dug underneath them to the bedrock: "none of us lives to himself." The question of food or feasts only matters because of a deeper question — *whose* are you? The setting matters because it shows that Christian living is never about fine-tuning our own preferences; it is about a Christian's deepest identity. If you belong to the Lord, then the Lord gets the say.

The law lands first. By nature we all live as though we were our own — self-ruled, self-directed, self-defending. Even after coming to Christ, the old man still reaches for the deed to your life, spending his days and decisions on himself: my comfort, my reputation, my way. But Scripture will not let us keep the deed. "You are not your own, for you were bought with a price" (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). To live for yourself is not freedom; it is a denial of the purchase. The law exposes the thief in us — we want to keep what Christ has paid for, as though His blood bought us a pardon but left us the owners.

But hear the gospel: "So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's." Your belonging to Him is not up for daily negotiation. The price was paid in full at the cross, and it is not payable in installments by your obedience. The One who owns you is not a hard master who squeezes value from His property; He is the Savior "who loved me and gave himself for me" (Galatians 2:20). Belonging to Him is your safety, not your bondage: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand" (John 10:28). If God "did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?" (Romans 8:32). To be owned by Christ is to be held by the One who will never drop you.

The doctrine underneath is the Christian's comfort in union with Christ. In 1563, Elector Frederick III of the Palatinate asked two young theologians — Zacharius Ursinus, a 28-year-old professor, and Caspar Olevianus, a pastor — to write a catechism that would unite his people and anchor them against Rome's errors. They opened it with the most searching question in all of Christian teaching: "What is your only comfort in life and in death?" The answer: "That I am not my own, but belong — body and soul, in life and in death — to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ." They wrote those words while their own land was torn by division, and men and women who had lost homes and livelihoods for the gospel clung to that comfort. No fire could burn it and no sword could cut it — because it rested not on their hold on Christ, but on His hold on them. John Calvin had made it his life's motto: *we are not our own* — and therefore, he said, let us not live or die for ourselves, but for God.

This is the day the LORD has made (Psalm 118:24), and His mercies are new this morning (Lamentations 3:22–23) — not because you belong to yourself and managed yesterday well, but because you belong to the Lord and He is faithful. Whether you live today or die today, you are His. Walk into the day owned, kept, and loved.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self's claim of ownership — the habit of spending your hours, your words, and your worries as though your life were your property to manage. That is the slave-market instinct of the flesh, and it always ends in anxiety or pride. *Put on* the comfort of belonging: this morning, lay the day's decisions, the day's fears, and the day's outcomes in the hands of your Owner, and live for Him on purpose — "So glorify God in your body" (1 Corinthians 6:20).

**Prayer:** Lord Jesus, my faithful Savior, thank You that I am not my own. You loved me and gave Yourself for me, and You have purchased me with Your blood — body and soul, in life and in death. Forgive me for living as though I still belonged to myself. Teach me to rest in my only comfort: that I am Yours, and nothing can snatch me from Your hand. Let this day be lived for You, and let my life and death alike bring You glory. In Your name I pray. Amen.

reflect.q: For reflection today
reflect.a: Where in your life are you still acting like the owner — holding the deed to your time, your plans, your future — and what changes when you hand that deed back to Christ?

devotionals.title: Not One Sparrow Falls
devotionals.verse: Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows.
body: "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows." — Matthew 10:29–31

Jesus spoke these words in Matthew 10, at the sending of the Twelve. He had just warned them plainly: they would be handed over to courts, flogged in synagogues, hated by all for His name's sake. He did not send them out with a promise of safety; He sent them out with a promise of the Father. Sparrows — the cheapest birds in the market, two for a penny — and not one of them falls apart from your Father. The setting matters: this is not a word for comfortable men, but for disciples walking into trouble. Providence is not God's hobby; it is the ground of courage.

The law lands first, right where we live. We plan and we worry; we lie awake rehearsing tomorrow's outcomes as though the world turned on our management of it. The old man wants to be his own providence — counting, controlling, securing — and the result is always the same: either anxious striving or weary despair. "And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" (Matthew 6:27). Worry is practical atheism: it confesses with our restlessness what we deny with our lips — that the Father might be looking the other way.

But hear the gospel: not one sparrow falls apart from your Father. The phrase carries the full weight — without His will, without His knowledge, without His care. If His eye is on the sparrow, His heart is on you; the hairs of your head are not merely counted but numbered, as a shepherd numbers his sheep, one by one, by name. Providence does not mean nothing hard will ever happen — the Twelve were promised suffering, not spared from it — but that nothing happens apart from your Father. There is no falling outside His hands.

The doctrine underneath is the providence of God: that the Almighty upholds and governs all things — "heaven and earth and all creatures," as the Heidelberg Catechism says (Q&A 27), so that "not a hair can fall from my head" without the will of my heavenly Father (Q&A 28). This was the Puritan John Flavel's lifelong meditation. Preaching in Devon through persecution, fines, and exile, he wrote *The Mystery of Providence*, tracing how God performs in the small turns of a life exactly what He purposed from eternity. He urged believers to keep a written record of God's providences — arguing that a remembered providence becomes a future anchor: what He governed yesterday proves He governs today. Calvin taught the same settled confidence: nothing happens by blind chance; what befalls the believer befalls him by the will and wisdom of a Father.

This is the day the LORD has made (Psalm 118:24), and His mercies are new this morning (Lamentations 3:22–23) — ordered, measured, and sent by the same Father who numbers the sparrows. Walk into it fearing not: you are of more value than many sparrows.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self's anxious self-providencing — the midnight rehearsals, the white-knuckled planning, the habit of carrying tomorrow's weight as though God had dropped it. That is the flesh trying to sit on the throne, and it always ends in anxiety or exhaustion. *Put on* the new-self confidence of a child under the Father's eye: plan your day honestly, work it diligently, and rest the outcomes in His hands, remembering that whatever meets you there has passed through His will first.

**Prayer:** Father, forgive my anxious striving. You know the fall of every sparrow and the number of every hair on my head — teach me to fear not, but to trust. Whatever this day holds, it holds me only as Your child, kept in the hand of Christ. Let my heart rest in Your providence, and let my life declare that nothing is too small for Your care. In Jesus' name, Amen.

reflect.q: For reflection today
reflect.a: What one worry are you carrying that belongs in the Father's hands — and what would it look like to do your part today and leave the outcome to Him?

devotionals.title: That You May Know
devotionals.verse: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.
body: "I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life." — 1 John 5:13

John wrote his first letter to churches shaken by false teachers — men who denied that Jesus had come in the flesh and then walked out of the fellowship, "that it might become plain that they all are not of us" (1 John 2:19). Imagine the questions left behind: Are we the true ones? How do we know? So the aged apostle writes the whole letter as a kind of examination — do you believe that Jesus is the Christ, do you keep His commandments, do you love the brethren — and then lands his purpose in one sentence: you can *know*. Not guess. Not hope against hope. Know.

The law lands first, right where many of us live. We stake our certainty on the weather of our hearts — a good day of prayer and we feel saved; a hard fall and we feel lost. The old self loves a ledger: my mood today, my record this week, my feelings as the final judge of my soul. But feelings are weather, not ground. "Whenever our heart condemns us," John says, "God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything" (1 John 3:20). If your assurance stands on your temperature, it will rise and fall with it — and you will spend your days re-trying to earn a verdict God already rendered.

Here is the gospel: assurance is built on God's testimony, not on your temperature. John grounds it in three immovable things. First, God's promise: the One who cannot lie has said the believer has eternal life, and His word is final. Second, Christ's finished work: your confidence before God rests on the blood and righteousness of Jesus, not on the steadiness of your devotion. Third, the Spirit's seal: "when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance" (Ephesians 1:13–14). A guarantee is not a maybe. Nothing — "neither death nor life, nor things present nor things to come, nor anything else in all creation" — can separate you from the love of God in Christ Jesus your Lord (Romans 8:38–39).

The doctrine underneath is the assurance of faith — and the Reformed confessions treat it as a real doctrine, not a personality trait. The Westminster Confession (ch. 18) teaches that a true believer "may be certainly assured that they are in the state of grace, and may rejoice in the hope of the glory of God," grounded on God's promises, the Spirit's testimony, and the evidence of grace in a holy life. This was no abstract comfort for John Bunyan. The tinker-turned-preacher wrestled for years in the dungeon of doubt — his *Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners* records the war within — until he learned to answer every accusing thought with God's promise rather than his feelings. He then wrote *Come and Welcome, to Jesus Christ* to drag others out of the same pit: Christ receives all who come, and He turns away none.

This is the day the LORD has made (Psalm 118:24), and His mercies are new this morning (Lamentations 3:22–23) — including the mercy of settled certainty. You need not face the day with a question mark over your head. Preach to your soul as the psalmist did — "Hope in God" (Psalm 42:11) — and let God's testimony have the last word.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self's habit of measuring your standing before God by the barometer of your feelings — today's temperature, yesterday's failure, the ledger of moods. *Put on* the settled posture of faith: come to the Word and let God's testimony be the judge of your soul, resting your whole weight on Christ's finished work and the Spirit's seal.

**Prayer:** Father, forgive me for asking my feelings to settle what only Your word can settle. You have said it: whoever believes in Your Son has eternal life. Anchor my heart to that promise today. When the accuser whispers, let me answer with Christ's finished work; when my heart condemns me, remind me that You are greater than my heart. Let my life this day declare what I know — that I am Yours, kept by grace, for the glory of Christ alone. In Jesus' name, Amen.

reflect.q: For reflection today
reflect.a: What one promise of God will you stake your certainty on today — and what would change if you truly believed you *know* you have eternal life?

devotionals.title: You Must Be Born Again
body: *"And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes and be careful to obey my rules."* — Ezekiel 36:26–27 (ESV)

God spoke these words to Israel in exile — a people whose hearts had hardened through generations of idolatry, who had profaned His name among the nations. They were not one good choice away from restoration. They were spiritually dead in a foreign land. And into that ruin God speaks in the first person: *I will* give, *I will* remove, *I will* put. The new heart is not a reward for the repentant; it is the cause of repentance. Centuries later, Nicodemus — a teacher of Israel, a moral man, a seeker in the night — heard the same word from Jesus' own mouth: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3, ESV). If the religious insider needed it, so does everyone.

Here is the law, and it lands first: you cannot re-birth yourself. A heart of stone does not soften by effort, by resolution, by programs, or by time. You know that road, Lewis — thirty-plus years of trying everything the world offered, and nothing worked, because the problem was never a lack of trying; it was a dead heart. Every morning the old man still wants to polish the stone: *this time my willpower will hold, this time I'll manage the sin.* But stone does not beat, no matter how well you polish it. "The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit" (John 3:8, ESV). You do not command the wind. You receive it.

And here is the gospel: *I will.* The whole verse is God's doing — the giving, the removing, the putting of His Spirit within. This is *sola gratia* at its deepest: regeneration is God's work alone, purchased by Christ alone, applied by the Spirit alone. God changed your life in that men's discipleship program when you believed John 17 — not because you finally found the right method, but because He removed the stone and gave you flesh. And the promise does not end there: He who began the good work will complete it. The new heart's proof is not perfection but direction — He *causes* you to walk in His statutes. Obedience is the fruit of the new birth, never its price. So this morning is not a call to try harder; it is a call to live from the heart He already gave you, by the Spirit He already put within you, for His glory alone.

The church has always confessed this. George Whitefield, the great evangelist of the Great Awakening, preached his most famous sermon — "You Must Be Born Again" — hundreds of times on both sides of the Atlantic, to coal miners in open fields and crowds in London. He watched respectable, church-going people weep because he told them what Jesus told Nicodemus: morality is not the new birth, religion is not the new birth, and no man can give it to himself. The Spirit gives life, and He gives it freely.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self's stone-polishing — the quiet belief that today's holiness depends on today's willpower, that if you manage yourself well enough God will be pleased. That is the flesh trusting the flesh, and it ends in pride or despair. *Put on* the new-self dependence of a heart of flesh: begin the day confessing you need the Spirit's wind again, then walk in His statutes from gratitude — not to earn the new heart, but because it is yours. "This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it" (Psalm 118:24), and His mercies are new this morning (Lamentations 3:22–23) — including the mercy of a heart that beats for Him.

**Prayer:** Father, great is Your faithfulness — mercies new this morning, and a heart of flesh where there was stone. Forgive me for the days I trust my own polishing. Keep me from the old man's self-reliance, and cause me to walk in Your statutes today by Your Spirit, in the name of Jesus, who gave Himself to make this new birth mine. Amen.

reflect.q: For reflection today
reflect.a: Where are you still trying to soften stone — managing a sin by willpower, carrying a burden by self-effort — instead of asking the Spirit to do what only He can do?

devotionals.title: Be Killing Sin
body: *"Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry."* — Colossians 3:5 (ESV)

Paul wrote these words to the Colossians around AD 60–62, a church of Gentile believers being courted by a philosophy that mixed Christ with ascetic rules and secret wisdom. His answer is not a new set of rules — it is a new identity. The chapter opens with the ground under the command: "If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above" (3:1), "for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (3:3). The command to kill sin does not come before the death to sin; it comes after it. You do not put sin to death to become God's child. Because you are dead to sin and alive in Christ, you may now put sin to death.

Here is the law, and it lands first: sin is still in you. Justification settled your standing forever, but the old self's corruption remains like an enemy hiding in a conquered city — and it is not content to hide. Paul names it without flinching: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, covetousness — "which is idolatry," because every sin is worship of something besides God. You know this war, Lewis — thirty-plus years before Christ taught you that the flesh is not a friend to be managed but an enemy to be put to death. And even now the old man whispers the same lie he always has: *manage it, hide it, feed it just a little — no one will know.* But sin tolerated is sin crowned. It does not stay small. It grows.

And here is the gospel: you are already dead to it. "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" (Romans 6:11). The cross is not only your pardon; it is your power. Christ did not merely forgive the sinner and leave him in the fight alone — He united you to Himself, so that His death to sin is your death to sin. Mortification is not moral striving to earn God's favor; it is the fruit of grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone. You kill sin by reckoning — counting true what God has declared true — and by the Spirit: "if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13). The Spirit does the killing; your work is to bring the knife — prayer, the Word, confession, flight from temptation — and let Him wield it.

The church has always confessed this. John Owen, the great Puritan theologian, wrote *Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers* in 1656 to Christians who, like us, assumed that once converted they were done with sin. His famous warning still stands: "Be killing sin or it will be killing you." Owen's method was no mere willpower. Watch sin daily, he said. Trace it to its roots. Starve what feeds it. And above all, bring it to the cross — because only the one who knows his forgiveness dares to look his sin in the face. Owen understood what Paul taught: mortification is the Spirit's work in the already-justified, aimed at the holiness "without which no one will see the Lord" (Hebrews 12:14) — all to the glory of God alone.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self's management of sin — the quiet negotiations, the secret feeding, the self "which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24): "put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), and "walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh" (Galatians 5:16). This is the day the LORD has made (Psalm 118:24); His mercies are new this morning (Lamentations 3:22–23) — including the mercy of a Spirit who fights with you.

**Prayer:** Father, great is Your faithfulness — mercies new this morning, and a life hidden with Christ in God. Forgive me for managing what You command me to kill. By Your Spirit, put to death what is earthly in me; teach me to reckon myself dead to sin and alive to You. Make me holy, for Your glory alone, in Jesus' name. Amen.

reflect.q: For reflection today
reflect.a: Name the one sin you have been managing instead of mortifying. What feeds it — and what would it look like to starve that today, by the Spirit?

devotionals.title: Grafted Into Christ
body: *"Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me. I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing."* — John 15:4–5 (ESV)

Jesus spoke these words in the upper room on the night before the cross, walking with His disciples toward Gethsemane and, beyond it, to His death. In hours He would be betrayed, denied, and crucified; they would be scattered, frightened, and hiding. It was no moment for abstractions. So He gave them a picture they could not forget: a vine and its branches. A branch does not negotiate its connection to the vine. It does not earn the sap, or schedule a season of fruitfulness by its own effort. Cut off, it withers; joined, it lives. And the joining is not the branch's doing — a vine does not graft itself.

Here is the law, and it lands first: "apart from me you can do nothing." Nothing. Not some things, not less than we hoped — nothing. The old self hears that sentence and tries to argue with it. It invents a middle ground: surely I can manage a little fruit on my own — a bit of patience here, a touch of kindness there, with Christ supplying what I lack. But the text leaves no room for partnership. A severed branch contributes exactly nothing to the vine. You know this temptation well, Lewis — the quiet habit of pressing on in your own strength, of treating Christ as the helper of your efforts rather than the source of your life. Every branch that tries to bear fruit apart from the vine ends the same way: dry, brittle, and gathered for the fire.

And here is the gospel: you did not graft yourself into Christ — He grafted you in. Union with Christ is God's own work, and it is the very hinge on which the whole of salvation turns. John Calvin, writing in the Institutes, put it with an edge: "As long as Christ remains outside of us, and we are separated from him, all that he has suffered and done for the salvation of the human race remains useless and of no value to us." But Christ does not remain outside of us. By His Spirit, the Father has united you to the Son — so truly joined that His death is your death and His life is your life. Justification, sanctification, adoption, resurrection — Paul's whole list of saving benefits comes to us in one package, because we receive them all *in Him*. This is grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, to the glory of God alone: a sinner who could do nothing is united to a Savior who has done everything, and the branch now draws sap from a living Vine.

That is why fruitfulness is a promise, not a pressure. "Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit." Notice who abides in whom first: He in you. The sap flows because the union holds — and the union holds because Christ holds it. Your part is not to manufacture fruit but to remain — to keep coming to the Vine in the Word, in prayer, in the means He appointed, the way a branch simply stays where it was grafted.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self's self-sufficiency — the severed-branch confidence that you can produce love, joy, peace, patience, and holiness by effort and resolve, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24): come to the Vine empty each morning and draw what you cannot make. This is the day the LORD has made (Psalm 118:24); His mercies are new this morning (Lamentations 3:22–23) — including the mercy of sap already flowing from Christ to you.

**Prayer:** Father, great is Your faithfulness — mercies new this morning, and a life already grafted into Your Son. Forgive me for the severed-branch strivings, the hours I tried to bear what only You can grow. Keep me joined to Christ; let His life flow through me today and bear fruit that points to Him alone, to Your glory alone. In Jesus' name, Amen.

reflect.q: For reflection today
reflect.a: Where are you trying to produce fruit apart from the Vine — gritting your teeth where you should be abiding? What would it look like to stay connected there today instead?

devotionals.title: Dead, Not Just Wounded
body: *"And you were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience — among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the body and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind."* — Ephesians 2:1–3 (ESV)

Paul wrote these words from a Roman prison around AD 60–62 to Christians in Ephesus — a city where he had once preached for two years, where the worship of Artemis filled the streets, and where these very believers had themselves been lost in the dark before Christ found them. He is not describing outsiders. "Among whom *we all* once lived," he says — apostles included. And notice the word he refuses to soften: *dead*. Not sick. Not wounded. Not struggling. Dead.

Here is the law, and it lands before the gospel does: the fall went all the way down. When Adam sinned, sin came into the world through one man, and death spread to all men because all sinned (Romans 5:12). Scripture is relentless about the depth: "The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5), and "the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9). Not some intentions. Not part of the heart. The corruption reaches the mind, the will, the affections — everything we use to try to climb out of it. That is why the old self's favorite project is self-repair. You know it, Lewis: thirty-plus years of trying everything the world offered — rehabs, programs, resolve, willpower — and nothing worked. What feels like discipline can be just another form of dying. A corpse cannot resuscitate itself, however sincere the effort.

This is the doctrine the church calls total depravity — the first truth of the Reformation's order of grace, enshrined in the Canons of Dort. It does not mean every person is as bad as he could possibly be. It means sin has touched every part of us, so that without God's work we cannot so much as move toward Him. In the early 400s, a British monk named Pelagius taught the opposite: that man is born neutral, that Adam's fall left us mostly fine, and that with enough effort anyone can live without sin and earn heaven. Augustine of Hippo answered him with Scripture — dead is dead. The church sided with Augustine at the Council of Carthage in 418, and the Reformers stood in that same line eleven centuries later: Luther, Calvin, and the whole Reformation confessed that salvation must be by grace alone, because dead men contribute nothing but the sin that made saving necessary.

And here is the gospel, and it comes on God's side of the ledger: *"But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved"* (Ephesians 2:4–5). The two most hopeful words in the Bible are "But God." He did not wait for the corpse to twitch. He did not send advice to the graveyard. He came Himself, in Christ, and made the dead alive. That is why your standing with the Lord rests on the truth of His Word, not on your feelings — a resurrection is not a mood. This is the day the LORD has made (Psalm 118:24), and His mercies are new this morning (Lamentations 3:22–23) — including the mercy that what Christ made alive, He keeps alive.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self's self-repair instinct — the daily temptation to believe you can be good enough, steady enough, disciplined enough to earn God's favor or finish what Christ started, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22). *Put on* the new self's honest dependence, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24): confess the deadness, and receive the life — this morning and every morning — as the gift it has always been.

**Prayer:** Father, great is Your faithfulness — mercies new this morning, and life given to the dead. Forgive me for the self-repair projects, the years and days I tried to earn what only You can give. You did not wait for me to get better; You made me alive in Christ. Keep me from Pelagius's old lie today, and let every breath of obedience be gratitude, not bargaining. To Your glory alone, in Jesus' name, Amen.

reflect.q: For reflection today
reflect.a: Where are you still trying to resuscitate yourself — to earn by effort what God has already given by grace? What would it look like to lay that project down and be made alive by Him today?

devotionals.title: By Grace, Through Faith
body: *"For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them."* — Ephesians 2:8–10 (ESV)

Yesterday we stood at the grave: dead in trespasses and sins, by nature children of wrath. Today Paul will not let us stay there. He picks up the same sentence he started in verse 5 — *"by grace you have been saved"* — and now he slows down to make sure we feel the weight of every word. *By grace.* *Through faith.* *Not your own doing.* *The gift of God.* *Not a result of works.* *So that no one may boast.* He stacks the phrases like stones in a wall, because he knows the old self will try to smuggle one brick of self-reliance through the gate.

Here is the law, and it cuts the pride before the gospel heals the wound: boasting is the native language of the fallen heart. The Pharisee in Jesus' parable prayed "with himself" — *God, I thank you that I am not like other men* (Luke 18:11). That is the old self talking, and it talks in all of us. It whispers that your thirty-plus years of wreckage were somehow worse than another man's respectable self-righteousness — or, just as deadly, that your years of faithfulness since have somehow earned you a standing the new believer doesn't have. Both are the same lie: that salvation is a wage. But a wage can be boasted about, and Paul says God designed salvation so that boasting is impossible. *"So that no one may boast."* If you contributed even a fraction, you could claim a fraction of the glory. God left no fraction.

This is the doctrine the Reformers recovered at the cost of everything: *sola gratia*, grace alone, and *sola fide*, faith alone. In 1517, when Luther nailed his Ninety-five Theses to the church door at Wittenberg, the fight was over indulgences — the church selling God's forgiveness for coins. But underneath was the deeper question: does anything in us complete what Christ began? The Council of Trent would later answer yes, anathematizing anyone who said otherwise. The Reformers answered with Ephesians 2: faith itself — even the *through faith* — is "not your own doing; it is the gift of God." You did not generate the hand that received the gift; God gave you the hand too. That is why your standing with the Lord rests on the truth of His Word, not on your feelings: feelings fluctuate, but a gift already given cannot be ungiven by a bad morning.

And here is the gospel, and it moves: *"For we are his workmanship."* The Greek word is *poiēma* — we are His poem, His crafted work. You are not God's employee, hired for good works; you are God's artwork, created *for* good works. The order matters more than anything: works do not make the poem, the Poet makes the poem, and then the poem walks. *"Which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them."* Before you were born, before you ever believed, God had already laid out the good works of this Tuesday — the recording, the encouragement, the faithfulness in small things — and prepared you to walk in them. You do not walk to become His workmanship. You walk because you are.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self's wage-earning — the quiet bookkeeping that measures today's devotion against yesterday's failure and decides whether God is pleased with you, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22). *Put on* the new self's received identity, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24): you are His workmanship, full stop — and today's good works are a walk He prepared, not a wage you earn.

**Prayer:** Father, I bring You no wage and no boast — only the empty hands You filled. Thank You that even my faith is Your gift, that I am Your workmanship and not my own project. Forgive the bookkeeping, the quiet pride that measures and compares. You prepared today's works beforehand; give me grace to simply walk in them, to Your glory alone. In Jesus' name, Amen.

reflect.q: For reflection today
reflect.a: Where are you still keeping spiritual books — tallying effort, weighing worthiness? What would it change to walk today's prepared works as His poem rather than His employee?

devotionals.title: Counted Back: Not One Written Off
devotionals.verse: 30 basins of gold, 1,000 basins of silver, 29 censers, 30 bowls of gold, 410 bowls of silver, and 1,000 other vessels; all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400
body: *"And this was the number of them: 30 basins of gold, 1,000 basins of silver, 29 censers, 30 bowls of gold, 410 bowls of silver, and 1,000 other vessels; all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400. All these did Sheshbazzar bring up, when the exiles were brought up from Babylonia to Jerusalem."* — Ezra 1:9–11 (ESV)
Some things get carried off so far from where they belonged that everybody stops expecting them back.

That is exactly what happened to the vessels of God's house. In 586 BC Nebuchadnezzar's army cut the great bronze pillars in pieces and carried the gold and silver vessels of the temple to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13-17). A generation later a Babylonian king was drinking wine out of them at a feast, praising gods of gold and silver (Daniel 5:2-4) — and that night he was weighed in the balances and found wanting (Daniel 5:27). What God had set apart as holy, men treated as common. That is the bad news, and it has to be said plain: God counts how His holy things — and His people — are handled.

But God had already spoken the end of the story before the exile was over: "They shall be carried to Babylon, and there they shall be until the day when I visit them, declares the LORD. Then I will bring them up and restore them to this place" (Jeremiah 27:22).

Seventy years ran out, and Cyrus sent the vessels home. Ezra does not wave at the number — he signs for it, piece by piece: "30 basins of gold, 1,000 basins of silver, 29 censers, 30 bowls of gold, 410 bowls of silver, and 1,000 other vessels; all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400" (Ezra 1:9-11). Counted out. Counted back. By number.

Here is the word to carry today: the vessels were *formed* before they were ever carried off. The Hebrew word for God's forming of man is **yatsar** (yaw-TSAR) — the potter's word: "then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground" (Genesis 2:7). You were not manufactured and misplaced. You were formed by hand — and the Hand that formed you is the same Hand that keeps the count. Captivity did not change the vessels' identity, and exile did not reduce their number. What God counts, He keeps.

The Reformers called this God's work under its opposite — Luther's theology of the cross: God does His strongest work hidden inside what looks like loss. The vessels looked lost in Babylon. They were, the whole time, on an inventory God Himself was keeping. Sola gratia — by grace alone — is not God hoping you make it back. It is God bringing His own home, every one accounted for. Soli Deo Gloria.

So if you feel like a vessel carried a long way from where you belonged, hear Ezra 1 as God's answer over your life: He has not lost count of you. Not one of His own is written off — and that includes the one reading this.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self's verdict that exile is final — the belief that being carried off, broken, or long away means you have been written off, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24): you are a vessel formed by the Potter's hand and counted by name, and you put away the old lie — "put off" falsehood and the old ways (Colossians 3:8-9) — having "put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10).

**Prayer:** Father, You formed me by hand and You have not lost count of me. When I feel carried far from where I belonged, remind me that Your promise was spoken before the exile ended, and that what You count, You keep. Keep me in Your hand today, and bring my heart home to You again. In Jesus' name, Amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Where were the vessels promised back — before or after the exile ended?
reflect.a: Before. God spoke the restoration in Jeremiah 27:22 while the vessels were still in Babylon. His promise over His people does not wait for circumstances to improve first.

reflect.q: Why does Ezra give the exact count — 5,400 — instead of just saying "the vessels returned"?
reflect.a: Because the count is the comfort. God keeps His inventory by number (Ezra 1:9-11), which means no single vessel — and no single person — is lost in the general story. He knows His own individually.

reflect.q: What do I do today if I feel carried off and counted out?
reflect.a: Come back to the Potter's hand. The marred vessel in Jeremiah 18:4 was reworked *in the potter's hand* — it never left his hands between the marring and the making. Staying in His hand, not fixing yourself first, is the way home.

devotionals.title: 276 Out of 276
body: *"And so it was that all were brought safely to land."* — Acts 27:44 (ESV)
**The ship: lost. The souls: 276 out of 276.**
That is Luke's own arithmetic for the worst shipwreck in the Bible, and it is worth reading slowly, the way Luke recorded it — by the numbers:

- **Fourteen days** driven by the northeaster, until "neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned" (Acts 27:20). - **Twenty fathoms, then fifteen** (27:28) — the soundings in the dark, the bottom rising under the ship. - **Four anchors from the stern**, and prayer for day to come (27:29). - **276 persons in the ship** (27:37). - The promise, spoken *before* the wreck: "there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship" (27:22). - The wreck: "The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf" (27:41). - The outcome: "the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land" (27:44).

Hold the two columns side by side. What was lost: one ship, its cargo, its tackle, its wheat. What was saved: every person on board — not 275, not most. All. That is the bad news and the good news in one record: Scripture does not pretend the vessel held. It broke. But the promise was never that the ship would hold — the promise is that God's people would.

The word for today is **ankyra** (ANG-koo-rah) — the Greek word for *anchor*, the word Hebrews uses when it calls our hope "a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain" (Hebrews 6:19). A sailor's anchor goes down into the sea. Ours, as Luther pictured it, is cast the other way — up into heaven itself, where Jesus has already gone as a forerunner. It holds not because the water is calm, but because of where it is fastened. That is also the theology: *sola fide* — the promise was a word to be believed, not a condition to be met. Paul did not tell those 276 people to swim better. He told them God's word: "not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you" (27:34).

So name your own two columns today. The vessel that is breaking — the plan, the strength, the old way of living — may truly be lost. But some around you may float home on pieces of your wreck: your testimony is a plank God intends to use.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self that trusts only what it can hold together — the self that "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the panic and falsehood the storm stirs up (Colossians 3:8-9). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a self anchored to Christ, not to the vessel.

**Prayer:** Father, when the vessel breaks and the soundings keep rising, hold me fast to Your promise. Teach me to believe Your word in the dark, and use even the pieces of my wreck to bring others safely to shore. Keep my anchor where You have set it — in Christ, behind the curtain. In Jesus' name, Amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: In Acts 27, what exactly was lost, and what exactly was saved?
reflect.a: The ship and everything in her were lost (Acts 27:22, 41). All 276 persons were saved (27:37, 44). God let the vessel break and kept every soul — the wreck itself teaches what a safe arrival never could.

reflect.q: Do anchors stop storms?
reflect.a: No — the four anchors in Acts 27:29 held the ship off the rocks until daylight; they did not calm the sea. Our anchor of hope (Hebrews 6:19) works the same way: it does not end the storm, it stops the drifting.

reflect.q: What piece of my own wreckage could God use for somebody else?
reflect.a: The part you would most like to sink. "The rest on planks or on pieces of the ship" (Acts 27:44) — a testimony is wreckage held out to someone going under. Held out, not hidden, is how a plank saves.

devotionals.title: God of the Valleys Too
body: *"And a man of God came near and said to the king of Israel, 'Thus says the LORD, "Because the Syrians have said, 'The LORD is a god of the hills but he is not a god of the valleys,' therefore I will give all this great multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the LORD."'"* — 1 Kings 20:28 (ESV)

Start with one Hebrew word: **biq'ah** (bik-AH) — a wide, low valley, a plain between the hills. It is the word Scripture uses for the valley of dry bones, where Ezekiel watched a graveyard stand up (Ezekiel 37:1-2). And it stands behind the most insulting sermon ever preached against God — preached by an enemy king's army about the God of Israel:

Syria's theology was simple: God is regional. He is strong on the high places — the winning seasons, the answered prayers, the days you feel close to Him — but down in the low country, He is out of His jurisdiction. So Syria moved the battle to the plain, expecting to fight Israel alone.

Here is the bad news, said plain: we believe Syria's sermon more often than we admit. On the mountain — clean, strong, provided for — God feels near. In the valley — the diagnosis, the relapse, the 3 a.m. dread, the season when heaven seems quiet — we quietly assume He does not work down here. That is the lie this verse was written to kill.

God did not defend His reputation from a mountaintop. He took the insult personally and went down into the valley to fight. Israel, hopelessly outnumbered, camped "like two little flocks of goats" — and in the low place, on the plain, God gave the great multitude into their hand (1 Kings 20:29). The victory happened exactly where Syria said God could not be.

And the lowest valley on the face of the earth tells the same story. The Jordan Valley is the deepest dry-land place on the planet — and that is precisely where the heavens opened and the Father's voice came down over the Son (Matthew 3:16-17). God keeps choosing the low ground. "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me" (Psalm 23:4) — David does not say God waits at the far end of the valley. He says God is in it, mid-walk, rod and staff in hand.

The Reformers had to unlearn Syria's theology too. The old religion sent men climbing — up monastery ladders, up pilgrim stairs — to find a God who lived at altitude. The Reformation put the pulpit back down in the valley: God is found where He has promised to be, in His Word, among ordinary people in low places. You do not have to climb out of your valley to reach Him. He has already come down into it.

So whatever your low place is this morning, hear 1 Kings 20:28 as God's own answer to the enemy's oldest lie: He is not a God of the hills only. He is God of the valleys too — this valley, your valley, today.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self that believes God is near only on good days — the self that "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the fear and falsehood the valley stirs up (Colossians 3:8-9). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a self that trusts God's promised presence in the low place, not feelings on the high place.

**Prayer:** Lord, I confess I have believed the lie that You are nearer on my good days than in my low places. Meet me in this valley the way You met Israel — not after I climb out, but right here, where I am. You are God of the hills and God of the valleys. I will fear no evil, for You are with me. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: What exactly did Syria claim about God, and why does it matter?
reflect.a: They claimed He was "a god of the hills but... not a god of the valleys" (1 Kings 20:28) — a limited, regional god. It matters because the same lie whispers to us: that God is present in our strong seasons and absent in our low ones.

reflect.q: Where did God choose to answer the insult?
reflect.a: In the valley itself. He gave Syria's army into Israel's hand on the plain (1 Kings 20:29), and at the lowest place on earth — the Jordan — the heavens opened over Jesus (Matthew 3:16-17). God does not avoid low ground; He works there.

reflect.q: What changes today if God is God of this valley too?
reflect.a: You stop waiting to feel "back on top" before you pray, hope, or obey. Psalm 23:4's comfort is not escape but presence — "you are with me" in the middle of the walk, not just at the end of it.

devotionals.title: The Mercy Seat: Where God Said "Meet Me There"
devotionals.verse: There I will meet with you
body: God gave Moses the measurements for the most guarded object on earth: "You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth. And you shall make two cherubim of gold... on the two ends of the mercy seat" (Exodus 25:17-18). About forty-five inches by twenty-seven — a slab of solid gold, hammered cherubim with wings stretched over it, resting on top of the ark, behind the thickest curtain in the world.
And then God said the most startling sentence in the whole blueprint: "There I will meet with you" (Exodus 25:22).

*"There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you about all that I will give you in commandment for the people of Israel."* — Exodus 25:22 (ESV)

The bad news stands in the same chapter, and it has to be faced: the meeting place was hidden. One curtain. One room. One man — the high priest — one day a year, and never without blood: on the Day of Atonement he sprinkled the blood of the sacrifice on and before the mercy seat, because the sins of the people stood between them and a holy God (Leviticus 16:14-15). Access to God was real, but it was narrow, bloody, and rare. Sin is not a small thing, and God never pretended otherwise.

Now hear the Greek word that carries the whole gospel in it: **hilastērion** (hee-las-TAY-ree-on). It is the word the New Testament uses for the mercy seat itself (Hebrews 9:5) — and it is the exact word Paul reaches for in Romans 3:25, where God "put forward" Christ Jesus "as a propitiation by his blood." A hilastērion. Paul is saying, in one word, that Jesus Christ is the mercy seat — the very place where God meets sinners, now no longer covered gold in a hidden room, but a crucified Savior lifted up in the open.

Because of that, the guarded sentence of Exodus became an open invitation: "Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need" (Hebrews 4:16). Notice — the throne did not stop being a throne. The mercy seat did not stop being holy. What changed is the door: the blood that used to be carried in once a year by one trembling man has been shed once for all by the Son Himself (Hebrews 10:19-20), and the invitation now runs to everyone who will come.

The Reformers recovered exactly this: no priestly class standing between you and the meeting place, no curtain you must wait behind while someone holier goes in — "there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5), and through Him every believer may come. Access is not arrogance. It is obedience to an invitation God wrote into the furniture of His own house: *Meet Me there.* Now the "there" is a Person, and He is not hidden.

So do not stand outside the curtain this morning, describing your need to the door. The mercy seat has a name, and He is risen. Draw near — with confidence, the Scripture says — and receive mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. Your time of need is exactly what the invitation was written for.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self that stands at a distance from God — treating prayer as a privilege for cleaner people — the self that "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the fear, falsehood, and uncleanness that keep you hiding behind the curtain (Colossians 3:8-9). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a self that comes boldly, honestly, and daily to the mercy seat Christ has opened.

**Prayer:** Father, thank You that You appointed a meeting place and then, in Christ, threw the door open. I come this morning not on my own record but on His blood — to receive mercy for yesterday and grace for today. Meet me here, as You promised. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Why was the mercy seat so guarded — one man, one day a year, only with blood?
reflect.a: Because God is holy and sin is real (Leviticus 16:14-15). The guard around the meeting place taught Israel — and teaches us — that access to God is never casual or cheap. The gospel does not lower the holiness; it provides the blood.

reflect.q: What does it mean that Christ is our hilastērion (Romans 3:25)?
reflect.a: The mercy seat was the one place where God's presence and man's sin met, covered by blood. Paul says God put Christ forward as that very place — in the open, once for all. Where God meets sinners now is a Person, not a hidden room.

reflect.q: What should I do with Hebrews 4:16 today?
reflect.a: Obey it literally: draw near with confidence — in prayer, today, about the specific need you have been only worrying about — expecting the two things the verse promises: mercy for what is behind you, and grace to help in time of need.

devotionals.title: What Does It Mean That Noah 'Found Grace'?
devotionals.verse: But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
body: It is the most important question hiding in the flood story, and most of us skim right past it: **what had Noah done to find grace?**

Read the page in order and the answer is unsettling. Genesis 6 opens with the worst report ever given on the human race: "The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5). God is grieved to His heart. Judgment is decreed on all flesh. And then — before Noah builds anything, preaches anything, or is called righteous anywhere — comes verse 8:
"But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD." (Genesis 6:8)

The Hebrew word is **chen** (khane) — grace, favor freely given, the kindness of the greater stooping toward the lesser who cannot earn it. Genesis 6:8 is the first place in the Bible where the word is *named*. Grace itself had already been *shown* — God was clothing Adam and Eve with His own hands back in Genesis 3:21, covering the very people who had just ruined everything — but here, on the darkest page of the Old Testament, grace gets its name. And notice the order, because the order is the whole doctrine: Noah's righteousness is only described *after* the grace, in verse 9. Grace first. Then the walking with God. Never the other way around.

The bad news has to stand, or grace means nothing: Noah lived in a world under a true verdict, and he was born into the same ruined race as everyone who drowned — "only evil continually" was the diagnosis of the species, not just of Noah's neighbors. Grace was not God noticing one good man in a bad world. Grace was God setting His favor on a sinner, and that favor — not Noah's record — is why there is a human race this morning.

Then comes the good news in the shape of an ark: the man who found grace built the vessel that carried life through judgment, and God shut him in Himself (Genesis 7:16). Eight souls, saved through water (1 Peter 3:20) — saved, every one of them, because grace had a name before it had an explanation.

Five hundred nine years ago today — October 31, 1517 — a German monk named Martin Luther nailed a protest to a church door in Wittenberg, because the church of his day had put grace up for sale: indulgences, coins in a chest, favor by purchase. The Reformation's answer was Noah's story recovered: *sola gratia* — grace alone. Not grace for sale, not grace for the impressive, not grace that starts after you clean up. Grace that finds you in a world under judgment, before you have done one thing to deserve it — and then teaches your hands to build.

So ask the question one more time, turned toward your own life: what had you done to find grace? Nothing. That is not the embarrassing part of the gospel. That is the gospel. "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God" (Ephesians 2:8). You did not find grace because you were findable. Grace found you because God is gracious — and the same chen that carried Noah through the flood carries His people still.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self that tries to earn God's favor — the record-keeping, self-justifying self that "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the anger, malice, and slander that belong to that old life (Colossians 3:8). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a self that receives grace as a gift and then, like Noah, walks with God and gets to work building.

**Prayer:** Lord, I did not find grace by being good, and I will not keep it by being impressive. Thank You that Your favor rested on me while I had nothing to offer but need. Teach me to live today the way Noah lived after verse 8 — not earning, but walking with You. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Where does grace first get its name in Scripture — and had it appeared before that?
reflect.a: The word chen is first named at Genesis 6:8, "Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD." But grace was shown earlier: in Genesis 3:21 God Himself clothed Adam and Eve after the fall. The word arrives later than the reality — grace was at work before it had a name tag.

reflect.q: Why does the order of Genesis 6:8-9 matter?
reflect.a: Grace is named in verse 8, before Noah's righteousness is described in verse 9. Favor comes first and produces the walking with God — the walking never produces the favor. Reverse the order and you have religion; keep it and you have the gospel.

reflect.q: What does Noah's grace have to do with Reformation Day?
reflect.a: Everything. Luther's protest on October 31, 1517 was against grace treated as something sold or earned. Sola gratia — grace alone — is Genesis 6:8 confessed by the church: God's favor rests on sinners freely, in Christ, before they have anything to show for themselves.

devotionals.title: Loved for No Reason in Us
body: Dear brother, dear sister,

I am writing to you this morning because so many of God's people quietly carry the same question: *Am I loved because of something in me — and what happens on the days when there is not much in me to love?* Moses answered that question for Israel in a letter you and I still need to read slowly:

*"It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers, that the LORD has brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt."* — Deuteronomy 7:7-8 (ESV)

Hear the bad news first, because the law will not let us skip it: Israel brought no reason with them. They were not numerous, not impressive, not strong — they were "the fewest of all peoples," a slave people with no record to present. And neither do we. Paul describes the people Christ died for with three honest words: weak, ungodly, sinners — "For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly" (Romans 5:6). If God's love had waited for a reason in us, it would still be waiting. Our lack of worth is real, and pretending otherwise helps no one.

Now hear the good news, and notice where Moses puts the ground: "it is because the LORD loves you." The reason for God's love is found in God — in His gracious character and His covenant promise — not in human worthiness. Jeremiah heard the same love speaking centuries later: "I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you" (Jeremiah 31:3). The Hebrew word behind that steadfast, promise-keeping kindness is **chesed** (kheh-SED) — covenant love that does not let go, because God has bound Himself to His people by promise. And Paul brings it to its sharpest point: "but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). The cross was planted before our improvement, not after it. This is *sola gratia* — grace alone. It removes boasting, because we contributed nothing that earned His love, and it removes despair, because our lack of worth was never the barrier we imagined.

John Calvin taught the church to rest here: God's love is free — the cause of our calling, not the effect of our loveliness. He does not find us worthy and then love us; He loves us, and in Christ makes us new. That is why your identity does not have to be rebuilt every morning from yesterday's performance. You approach God today on the basis of His promise — loved first, before you had anything to show.

So, beloved, rest your heart where Moses rested Israel's: not on a reason in you, but on a Redeemer given for you. The gospel does not say, "Become lovable and God may receive you." It says, "God loved you and sent Christ for you; come and be made new."

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self that keeps presenting its record to God — begging, bargaining, and measuring His love by your week — the self that "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the anger, wrath, and malice that belong to that old life of striving (Colossians 3:8). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a self that receives love as a gift and then loves others from that full supply.

**Prayer:** Father, thank You that Your love for me never waited for a reason in me. When I am tempted to earn what Christ has already secured, remind me that You loved me while I was still a sinner, and that Your promise — not my performance — is my standing today. Teach me to love others the way I have been loved: freely, first, and without keeping score. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
With love, and praying for you today,
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: What reason does Moses rule out for God's love — and what reason does he give instead?
reflect.a: He rules out anything in Israel: not their number, strength, or impressiveness — they were "the fewest of all peoples" (Deuteronomy 7:7). The reason he gives is in God Himself: "it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers" (Deuteronomy 7:8). God's love is grounded in His character and covenant, not in our worthiness.

reflect.q: What is chesed, and where do we hear it in this teaching?
reflect.a: Chesed is God's covenant steadfast love — loyal, promise-keeping kindness that does not let His people go. Jeremiah hears it as everlasting love that keeps drawing God's people: "I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you" (Jeremiah 31:3).

reflect.q: How does Romans 5:8 prove that God's love came before our improvement?
reflect.a: Because of the timing Paul insists on: "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." Christ did not die for people who had cleaned themselves up; He died for the weak, the ungodly, and sinners (Romans 5:6, 8). Love came first, and renewal follows it — never the other way around.

devotionals.title: The Valley of Dry Bones
devotionals.verse: And I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land. Then you shall know that I am the LORD; I have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD
body: Picture the scene first, because Ezekiel wants you to stand in it. "The hand of the LORD was upon me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of the LORD and set me down in the middle of the valley; it was full of bones" (Ezekiel 37:1). Not a few bones — a valley full of them, the remains of a slaughtered army. Ezekiel walked among them and reported what he saw: "they were very many in the valley, and behold, they were very dry" (Ezekiel 37:2). Very many, and very dry. Whatever life had once been in that place had been gone a long, long time.
Then God asked the question the whole chapter hangs on: "Son of man, can these bones live?" Ezekiel gave the only honest answer a man can give over a graveyard: "O Lord GOD, you know" (Ezekiel 37:3).

Hear the bad news first, because this valley will not let us soften it. Israel said of themselves, "Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost; we are indeed cut off" (Ezekiel 37:11) — and by every human measure, they were right. Dead things cannot revive themselves. Dry bones cannot decide to live, cannot try harder, cannot turn over a new leaf. And neither can a sinner dead in sin raise himself. If life was going to come to that valley, it had to come from outside the bones entirely. That is the law's honest verdict over every one of us: our dryness is real, and it is beyond our power to fix.

Now hear the good news, and notice how it came. God did not send the bones a pep talk; He sent His word and His Spirit. At God's command Ezekiel preached to the bones, and "bone came to its bone" — sinews, flesh, and skin covered them — "but there was no breath in them" (Ezekiel 37:7-8). Form without life is still a corpse. Only when the prophet prophesied to the breath, and the breath came into them, "they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army" (Ezekiel 37:10). The Hebrew word underneath both "breath" and "Spirit" here is **ruach** (ROO-akh) — breath, wind, Spirit — God's own life-giving breath, the same ruach that hovered over the waters at creation. And God sealed the promise in today's anchor: "And I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land. Then you shall know that I am the LORD; I have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD" (Ezekiel 37:14).

This is *sola gratia* in a valley: resurrection is not the resuscitation of the strong; it is God's breath in what everyone else has already buried. John Calvin taught the church to hold God's Word and God's Spirit together — the word preached does its life-giving work because the Spirit breathes through it, never apart from it. That is why this valley points straight to the empty tomb, and forward still to the day the graves open at the voice of the Son of God (John 5:28-29). It answers the addict, the prodigal, and everyone who has been written off: your dryness is not God's verdict on you. His question still stands over every hopeless place: "Can these bones live?" And His answer is a promise: "I have spoken, and I will do it."

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self that has made peace with the graveyard — the voice that says "Our hope is lost" and calls surrender to despair honesty, the self that "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the bitterness and wrath that belong to that old life (Colossians 3:8). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a self that expects God to do what only God can do, and stands up when His breath comes.

**Prayer:** Lord God, You know the dry places in my life — the hopes I have buried and stopped praying over. I cannot raise them, and I will not pretend I can. Speak Your word over them again, and put Your Spirit within me afresh, that I may live. You have spoken, and You will do it. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: What did Ezekiel see in the valley, and what question did God ask him?
reflect.a: He saw a valley full of bones — "very many" and "very dry" (Ezekiel 37:2), the remains of a slaughtered army long past human hope. God asked, "Son of man, can these bones live?" and Ezekiel answered, "O Lord GOD, you know" (Ezekiel 37:3).

reflect.q: Why did the bones need the breath after the flesh had come on them?
reflect.a: Because form without life is still a corpse: after bone, sinews, flesh, and skin came together, "there was no breath in them" (Ezekiel 37:8). Only when the ruach — God's breath, His Spirit — came into them did they live: "they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army" (Ezekiel 37:10). Outward change is not new life; God's Spirit is.

reflect.q: What promise does God Himself seal the vision with?
reflect.a: "And I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land. Then you shall know that I am the LORD; I have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD" (Ezekiel 37:14). The life of God's people rests on His spoken promise and His Spirit — not on any life left in the bones.

devotionals.title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
body: Paul ends the long history of God's vessels with a turn nobody expected. After the temple's gold, the counting out to Babylon, and the counting back — 5,400 vessels, not one written off — the apostle announces where God has now put His greatest treasure: *"But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us"* (2 Corinthians 4:7). Count it out with Paul, one truth at a time.

**1. The treasure is real, and it is not ours.** The treasure is the gospel itself — the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. We did not make it, earn it, or improve it. We received it. That is *sola gratia* in a clay pot: the most valuable thing on earth, handed to people who brought nothing to the exchange.

**2. The jar is clay — on purpose.** The Greek is *ostrakina skeuē* — unglazed, everyday, cheap clay pots. Not the temple's gold vessels. The kind of pot you could buy anywhere and break any day. And God chose *those* — deliberately — so that when the power shows, nobody credits the pot. Hear the bad news honestly first: left to ourselves, we are exactly that fragile. Paul counts the jar's condition without any varnish: "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed" (2 Corinthians 4:8-9). Four pressures, honestly named. The law will not let the jar pretend to be gold: our own strength cracks under far less than this.

**3. The power belongs to God — and that is the good news.** Read Paul's four pairs again and notice the second half of each one: afflicted, *but not crushed*; perplexed, *but not driven to despair*; persecuted, *but not forsaken*; struck down, *but not destroyed*. The jar survives not because clay is strong, but because the treasure's Keeper is. The surpassing power belongs to God and not to us — which means your weakness is not the disqualification you feared. It is the very setting God chose, so that His power, not your polish, gets the glory. *Soli Deo Gloria.*

Martin Luther saw this same pattern at the Heidelberg Disputation of 1518 and gave it a name the church still uses: the **theology of the cross**. God does His work under its opposite — strength hidden in weakness, life hidden in death, glory hidden in shame. A crucified Savior. A persecutor turned apostle — Paul himself, the "chosen vessel" of Acts 9:15, who knew exactly what he was talking about. A church of jars of clay. The container was never the point. The hands are the point. And a jar that stays in the Potter's hand, cleansed and set apart, becomes "a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work" (2 Timothy 2:21).

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self that is ashamed of being clay and keeps trying to pass itself off as gold — the self that "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the anger, wrath, and malice that crack the jar from the inside (Colossians 3:8). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a self content to be clay in the Potter's hand, so the treasure — not the jar — is what people see.

**Prayer:** Lord, I confess I have wished for gold when You chose to make me clay. Forgive my shame over the cracks, and teach me to glory in the truth Paul counted out: the treasure is Yours, the power is Yours, and the keeping is Yours. Hold this jar in Your hand today, and let the light of Christ shine through it to someone who needs hope. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.
