reflect.q: What is the treasure, and what kind of jar does God put it in?
reflect.a: The treasure is the gospel — the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. God puts it in *ostrakina skeuē*, unglazed, everyday, cheap clay pots (2 Corinthians 4:7) — ordinary, breakable people — on purpose, "to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us."

reflect.q: How does Paul count the jar's condition in 2 Corinthians 4:8-9?
reflect.a: In four honest pairs: "afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed." The pressure is real, and so is the keeping — the jar is held, not because clay is strong, but because God is.

reflect.q: What did Luther call this pattern at Heidelberg in 1518?
reflect.a: The theology of the cross: God does His work under its opposite — strength hidden in weakness, life hidden in death, glory hidden in shame. It is why a crucified Savior, a remade persecutor, and a church of clay jars can carry the greatest treasure in the world.

devotionals.title: The Ship That Almost Broke
devotionals.verse: But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up
body: What happens when a prophet runs from God — and who pays for the ticket? Jonah bought passage to Tarshish to flee his calling, and the sea found him out: "But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up" (Jonah 1:4). This was no accident of weather. It was pursuit.

How bad did it get before anyone told the truth? The mariners "hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for them" (Jonah 1:5), every sailor cried out to his own god, and the captain had to wake the one man asleep in the inner part of the ship. Lots were cast, and the lot fell on Jonah. Only then did he confess: "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land" (Jonah 1:9) — the Maker of the sea, fled from across it.

Hear the bad news plainly: sin is never private. Jonah's rebellion endangered every soul on board, and the honest human remedy failed — the sailors "rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea grew more and more tempestuous against them" (Jonah 1:13). Rowing harder does not calm a storm God has sent, and trying harder does not settle a conscience we are outrunning.

So what finally stopped the storm? Follow one Hebrew word through the chapter and you will see it. The verb is **tul** (tool) — to hurl, to cast violently. The LORD *hurled* the wind (1:4). The mariners *hurled* the cargo (1:5). Nothing worked until Jonah himself said, "Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you" (Jonah 1:12). And they did: "So they picked up Jonah and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging. Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows" (Jonah 1:15-16).

That is the good news in this near-wreck — and it points beyond Jonah. The ship did not break. The runner did, and every sailor came to fear the true God because of the storm. Jonah went down so the storm would stop; Jesus, the greater Jonah — "behold, something greater than Jonah is here" (Matthew 12:41) — went down under the storm of judgment itself and rose, so that runners could be brought home instead of lost at sea. That is *sola gratia*: sailors are not saved by better rowing, and we are not saved by better trying. We are saved because God pursues and brings His people through.

The Puritan pastor John Flavel (1627–1691) ministered in Dartmouth, a busy English seaport, and in *The Mystery of Providence* (1678) taught that no wind blows by chance: God's providence governs storms as surely as calms, and often uses the storm itself as mercy — to stop a runner and turn a whole crew toward God. A storm sent by God is not God giving up on you. Sometimes it is God refusing to let you go.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self that runs and then sleeps through the consequences — the self that "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the anger, wrath, and malice that belong to that old life (Colossians 3:8). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a self that stops running, tells the truth quickly, and trusts the God who pursues His own across any sea.

**Prayer:** Lord, You made the sea and the dry land, and there is nowhere my running could take me out of Your sight. Forgive me for the storms my disobedience has brought on others, and thank You that You pursued Jonah — and pursue me — instead of letting me go. Thank You for the greater Jonah, Jesus Christ, who went down so the storm would cease for sinners. Set my course toward You today, and keep me in Your hand. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Who sent the storm in Jonah 1, and how do we know this was no ordinary weather?
reflect.a: The LORD did: "the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up" (Jonah 1:4). The storm came because Jonah was running from God — it was pursuit, not chance — and it ceased the moment Jonah was cast into the sea (Jonah 1:15).

reflect.q: What does the repeated Hebrew word tul teach us about how the storm ended?
reflect.a: Tul (to hurl) runs through the chapter: the LORD hurled the wind (1:4), the mariners hurled the cargo (1:5), and Jonah finally said, "Pick me up and hurl me into the sea" (1:12). Hurling cargo could not save the ship; only when the man who caused the tempest was himself cast over did "the sea cease from its raging" (Jonah 1:15) — and the sailors came to fear the LORD (1:16).

reflect.q: Why could the sailors not save themselves by rowing, and where does Jonah point us?
reflect.a: Because "the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea grew more and more tempestuous against them" (Jonah 1:13) — human effort cannot calm a storm sent against sin. Jonah points to Jesus, of whom He said, "behold, something greater than Jonah is here" (Matthew 12:41): Christ went down under judgment and rose, so runners could be saved by grace, not by rowing.

devotionals.title: Booths: Built to Remember
devotionals.verse: You shall dwell in booths for seven days. All native Israelites shall dwell in booths, that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God
body: Once a year, God told His people to move out of their houses. Five days after the Day of Atonement, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, Israel kept the Feast of Tabernacles — seven days of celebration, with an eighth day of solemn assembly, at the very end of the harvest year. Every family built a booth, a rough shelter made from what God had listed: "the fruit of splendid trees, branches of palm trees and boughs of leafy trees and willows of the brook" (Leviticus 23:40), and lived in it for the week — eating, rejoicing, and sleeping under the branches. The command itself leaves no room to soften it into a symbol: "You shall dwell in booths for seven days. All native Israelites shall dwell in booths, that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God" (Leviticus 23:42-43).

Hear the bad news the booth was built to expose. A solid house can preach a lie. Walls, a roof, and a full barn quietly tell us we are secure because we built, earned, and stored — and prosperity has a way of erasing the memory of dependence. Israel in the wilderness had no house, no harvest, and no land; they lived because God sheltered them, fed them, and brought them out of Egypt. Settled in houses they did not build, the danger was never the booth. The danger was forgetting. Left to ourselves, we do not remember grace for long. We call our shelter our own work, and the God who carried us becomes a story we tell instead of the Lord we depend on. That is why the feast was not optional sentiment; it was a commanded return to the truth.

The Hebrew word underneath it is **sukkah** (sook-KAH) — a booth, a hut, a temporary shelter; its plural, *sukkot*, gives the feast its name. A sukkah was never meant to last. Its branches would wither, its roof would let the stars — and the rain — through, and that was the lesson in the building itself: this world’s shelters are temporary, and God’s people were pilgrims before they were householders. The meaning of Tabernacles, in the teaching this devotional is drawn from, is plain: the God who sheltered Israel in tents in the wilderness, with nothing, is the same God who shelters His people still.

Now hear the good news. It was at this feast, "on the last day of the feast, the great day," that Jesus "stood up and cried out, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water''" (John 7:37-38). And John opens his Gospel with the same tent-word in Greek: "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14) — He *tabernacled* among us. God did not only shelter His people from a distance; in Christ He came and lived in the shelter with them. The story ends where the booth was always pointing: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people" (Revelation 21:3). One day the temporary shelters come down forever, because God Himself moves in — and He never moves out. That is *sola gratia*: our lasting home is not built by our hands; it is given.

Matthew Henry (1662–1714), the Puritan-era pastor whose commentary generations have kept by the family Bible, taught readers of Leviticus 23 to see the booths as a lesson in holding this world’s comforts loosely and remembering the wilderness mercies of God — to live, even in a settled house, as people whose shelter has always been the Lord Himself. The booth is not nostalgia. It is theology you can sit under.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self that trusts the roof it built and forgets the God who sheltered it — the self that "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the self-reliance, ingratitude, and malice that belong to that old life (Colossians 3:8). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a self that remembers Egypt, remembers the wilderness, rejoices in the harvest without worshiping it, and rests in God as its true dwelling.

**Prayer:** LORD, You made Your people dwell in booths so they would never forget who brought them out of Egypt and who kept them in the wilderness. Forgive me for trusting the house instead of the God who sheltered me. Thank You that in Christ You tabernacled among us, and that Your final word is a dwelling that never comes down. Teach me to hold this world’s shelters loosely and to rejoice in You today. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: What did God command in Leviticus 23:42-43, and why?
reflect.a: "You shall dwell in booths for seven days. All native Israelites shall dwell in booths, that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God" (Leviticus 23:42-43). Every generation was to learn, by living it, that God Himself had sheltered Israel in the wilderness.

reflect.q: What does the Hebrew word sukkah teach us about the feast?
reflect.a: A sukkah is a booth — a temporary, fragile shelter of branches. Its withering roof was the lesson: earthly shelters do not last, God’s people are pilgrims, and their true shelter has always been the Lord who brought them out of Egypt.

reflect.q: Where do the booths finally point in Christ and in Revelation 21:3?
reflect.a: In Christ, who "tabernacled" among us — "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14) — and who, at this very feast, promised rivers of living water to whoever believes (John 7:37-38). And finally to the day when "the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people" (Revelation 21:3) — the temporary booth replaced by God’s permanent dwelling with His people.

devotionals.title: Erastus: The Name Rome Carved in Stone
devotionals.verse: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you
body: Count what is packed into one verse most readers skim on the way to the doxology: "Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you" (Romans 16:23). One verse. Three men named in it — and a fourth standing just behind it, for in the verse before, Tertius, the scribe who wrote Romans down at Paul's dictation, greets the church in his own name (Romans 16:22). Now count the names themselves: *Tertius* means "third," and *Quartus* means "fourth." Two men go down in Scripture remembered by numbers. One man is remembered by a job — "the city treasurer." One is remembered by hospitality — Gaius, the Gaius Paul baptized (1 Corinthians 1:14), under whose roof the whole Corinthian church met. No sermons from any of them are recorded. No miracles bear their names. And yet God breathed out every syllable of the roll call on purpose.

Then, in 1929, the stones began to talk. Excavators at Corinth — the city Paul was writing from when he penned Romans — uncovered a Latin pavement inscription recording that an Erastus laid that pavement at his own expense in return for his aedileship, a city office. Same name. Same city. Same era as Paul's city treasurer. One name, carried in two records: a stone a man paid for to honor himself in his city, and a verse God paid for — at the price of His Son — to honor a servant in His church. Scholars hold the identification as fitting rather than proven beyond question, and we hold it the same way. But even the possibility preaches: the pavement cracked and was buried for nineteen centuries, while the verse has been read aloud in the church without pause.

Hear the bad news first. Left to ourselves, we carve our own pavements. We want our names cut somewhere that lasts — in a title, a reputation, a following, a record of what we built — because deep down we fear we will be forgotten, and forgotten means worthless. That fear is the old self talking, and it drives the boasting, the self-promotion, and the quiet despair of ordinary believers who serve where nobody applauds. The law of God exposes it: worth that must be carved by our own hands is worth that crumbles with the stone.

Now the good news. Jesus told His rejoicing disciples to set their joy somewhere no excavation will ever need to find: "rejoice that your names are written in heaven" (Luke 10:20). The believer's name is not preserved because he was important; it is preserved because God is gracious — *sola gratia*, by grace alone. That is why Romans 16 can end the greatest letter ever written with a treasurer, a host, a scribe called Third, and a brother called Fourth. The Greek word behind "treasurer" is **oikonomos** (oy-kon-OM-os) — a steward, the manager of a household or a city, one trusted with what belongs to another. That is every Christian's true title. We own nothing; we are stewards of Another's goods, and a steward needs only one commendation — that the Master knows his name and finds him faithful where he was placed.

John Chrysostom (c. 349–407), the early church's great preacher, devoted a whole course of homilies to Romans and lingered over these closing greetings rather than skipping them, marveling that the apostle who carried nations on his heart still carried individual names there too — men and women the world would never record, recorded forever because heaven knew them. The roll call is not filler at the end of the letter. It is the doctrine of the church with names attached: Christ's body is made of hosts, treasurers, scribes, and brothers.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self that must be seen to believe it matters — the self that "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the boasting, bitterness, and self-seeking that belong to that old life (Colossians 3:8). *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a steward content to be known in heaven, faithful in the post God assigned — host, treasurer, scribe, or simply "the brother."

**Prayer:** LORD, You did not skip the names at the end of Romans, and You will not skip mine, because my name stands written in heaven by grace alone, not by anything I carved. Forgive me for chasing a pavement that will crack. Make me a faithful steward of what belongs to You, content to serve where You have placed me, and glad that You know my name. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Who is named in Romans 16:23, and how is each man remembered?
reflect.a: "Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you" (Romans 16:23). Gaius is remembered for hospitality, Erastus for his office as city treasurer, and Quartus simply as "the brother" — his name itself means "fourth."

reflect.q: What was found at Corinth in 1929, and how should we hold it?
reflect.a: A Latin pavement inscription recording that an Erastus laid the pavement at his own expense in return for his aedileship — the same name, city, and era as Paul's city treasurer. The identification fits well, but Scripture does not state it outright, so we hold it as likely, not proven.

reflect.q: Where does Jesus tell His people to ground their joy about their names?
reflect.a: In heaven's record, not earth's: "rejoice that your names are written in heaven" (Luke 10:20). A believer's name endures by grace alone, because God wrote it — not because the believer carved it.

devotionals.title: Written on Hearts, Not Stone
devotionals.verse: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and each his brother, saying, 'Know the LORD,' for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more
body: Read the promise slowly, phrase by phrase, the way Jeremiah's hearers had to — with Jerusalem under siege and the old covenant lying in ruins around them: "For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and each his brother, saying, 'Know the LORD,' for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more" (Jeremiah 31:33-34). Count the "I wills." God will put. God will write. God will be their God. God will forgive. God will remember no more. The verbs belong to Him from first to last.

Now hear the bad news the promise answers. The first covenant was written on stone, and stone was not the problem — the hearts beneath it were. Israel received the law on tablets at Sinai and broke it before Moses even came down the mountain, and Jeremiah's generation had done the same for centuries. The law written outside a man can accuse him, guide him, and expose him, but it cannot change him. Ezekiel named the condition plainly: a "heart of stone" (Ezekiel 36:26). A stone heart hears the command and does not move. Left to ourselves, that is every one of us — the commandment is holy and good, and we still cannot keep it from within.

The good news is that God did not promise to write louder on the stone. He promised a different location and a different work: "And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26). And at the Last Supper, Jesus lifted the cup and sealed Jeremiah's words in His own blood: "This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20). This is *sola gratia* — by grace alone. The believer does not climb up to God by a better performance under the old writing; God comes down and writes His law where the failure lived, forgiving iniquity first and remembering sin no more. Paul saw the finished work and called believers a letter "written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts" (2 Corinthians 3:3).

The Hebrew word for "heart" here is **leb** (layv) — not merely the seat of feeling, but the inner person himself: the mind that understands, the will that chooses, the conscience that answers. When God says He will write on the *leb*, He is not promising a stronger emotion about religion. He is promising a new inner person who knows Him — "from the least of them to the greatest" — and loves what He commands because the command now lives inside.

John Calvin (1509–1564), preaching and writing through the Reformation, insisted the new covenant was not a different way of salvation but the same covenant of grace now come in its fullness — God no longer dealing with His people at a distance through shadows, but pardoning their sin fully and renewing them by His Spirit from within. That is why the Reformed faith has always held both truths together: the pardon is complete and free in Christ alone, and the people pardoned are, by that same grace, made new.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the stone-heart habits that belong to it — the coldness, resentment, and disobedience Paul lists in Colossians 3:8. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a heart of flesh that hears God's law not as a threat from outside, but as the family likeness being written within.

**Prayer:** LORD, You said You would do this, and You have — You forgave, You remembered no more, and You put Your Spirit within Your people in Christ. Write Your law on my heart again today. Take away every cold and stony place in me, and make me glad to walk in what You command, not to earn Your love, but because I am already Yours. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: What does God promise to do in Jeremiah 31:33-34?
reflect.a: He promises a new covenant in which He will put His law within His people and write it on their hearts, be their God, forgive their iniquity, and remember their sin no more: "For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more" (Jeremiah 31:34).

reflect.q: How does Ezekiel describe the same promise?
reflect.a: As a heart transplant God Himself performs: "And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26).

reflect.q: Where was this covenant sealed?
reflect.a: At the Last Supper, in the blood of Christ: "This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20). The promise Jeremiah spoke, Jesus sealed.

devotionals.title: The First Promise in the Garden
devotionals.verse: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel
body: Begin at the beginning — not with the light and the garden at their best, but with the garden after everything broke. Adam and Eve had eaten what God forbade, and now they were hiding among the trees, sewing fig leaves, ashamed of the very goodness God had made. Into that hiding place God came, not first with a promise, but with a question and a curse — and then, speaking to the serpent who had deceived them, He said the first gospel word ever recorded: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel" (Genesis 3:15). Before there was a nation, a law, a temple, or a prophet, there was a promise — and it was spoken over a broken beginning.

Hear the bad news the promise answers, because the promise only shines against it. "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). Genesis does not let any of us stand outside the garden story as spectators. The hiding, the blame-shifting, the shame — that is our story too, written into every family wound and every wasted year. The law of God names it honestly: we fell in Adam, and left to ourselves we do not climb back. Fig leaves are still our first instinct, and fig leaves have never covered anything.

The good news is that God did not wait for Adam and Eve to fix their beginning before He began redemption. He announced the Seed before He drove them from the garden. That promised offspring runs through the whole book — foreshadowed in Isaac, the beloved son carried up Mount Moriah, and in Joseph, rejected by his brothers and sold, then raised up to save many lives. Jacob's ladder, reaching from earth to heaven, points to Him too, for Jesus Himself claimed it: "Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man" (John 1:51). At the cross the heel was truly bruised — the Seed suffered — but the serpent's head was crushed, and the empty tomb proves the bruising did not have the last word. This is *sola gratia*, by grace alone, and *solus Christus*, through Christ alone: the rescue was promised by God, and the rescue was accomplished by God, before we had anything to offer.

The Hebrew word for "offspring" here is **zera** (ZEH-rah) — seed, offspring, descendant. Paul lingers over its singular form when he writes of Abraham's promise: "It does not say, 'And to offsprings,' referring to many, but referring to one, 'And to your offspring,' who is Christ" (Galatians 3:16). The *zera* of the woman in Genesis 3:15 is not finally a crowd or a principle. He is a Person. The first promise in the garden was always pointing to Jesus by name.

Martin Luther (1483–1546), in his Lectures on Genesis, treated this verse the way the early church had — as the *protevangelium*, the first gospel, the mother promise from which every later promise in Scripture grows. Luther's point still steadies struggling believers: Adam and Eve walked out of the garden with nothing in their hands but a word from God, and that word was enough to live on. Faith, the Reformers insisted, is exactly that — clinging to God's promise in Christ when everything visible says the story is broken at the start.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away the garden's old habits that belong to it — hiding from God, blame-shifting, and the anger and malice Paul lists in Colossians 3:8. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): come out of hiding, confess plainly, and live today as one whose new beginning was given, not earned.

**Prayer:** LORD, You spoke a promise before You spoke an exile, and You have been keeping that promise ever since. When my beginning looks broken and my past looks wasted, teach me to cling to the Seed You promised — to Jesus, who was bruised for me and who crushed the serpent for me. Give me a new beginning today, not by my fixing, but by Your grace. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: What did God promise in Genesis 3:15?
reflect.a: He promised that the offspring of the woman would bruise the serpent's head, even as his own heel was bruised: "he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel" (Genesis 3:15).

reflect.q: Who is the promised offspring?
reflect.a: A single Person, not a crowd. Paul says the promise pointed to one offspring, "who is Christ" (Galatians 3:16) — the Seed promised in the garden is Jesus.

reflect.q: What does Genesis 3:15 say to a broken beginning?
reflect.a: That God was already writing redemption into page one. You do not have to fix your beginning for Him to give you a new one; the promise came first, and in Jesus that first promise became a Person you can trust today.

devotionals.title: Far Off — and Brought Near
body: Why does heaven sometimes seem silent? Have you ever prayed and felt as if you were praying at a wall — as if God were far off, and you were on the outside looking in? Isaiah tells Israel the honest reason, and it is not that God has grown weak or deaf: "Behold, the LORD's hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear dull, that it cannot hear, but your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear" (Isaiah 59:1–2). The question this verse forces is not, "Has God moved?" It is, "What has my sin done to the fellowship I was made for?"

Hear the bad news plainly, because the teaching names it without softening it. Sin's first damage is distance. It is the garden story all over again — Adam and Eve driven out, and at the east of Eden God placed "the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life" (Genesis 3:24). Paul describes the same condition: "separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world" (Ephesians 2:12). The misery of sin is not mainly that it makes us bad. It is that it makes us *far* — far from the God whose nearness is life itself. The law tells this truth about us, and left to ourselves we have no ladder long enough to climb back.

So where is the good news for the far off? It is not in a longer ladder. It is in a nearer Savior. "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ" (Ephesians 2:13). At the cross, Jesus cried, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — the distance sin makes, endured by the one Man who never earned it, so that distance could end for us. And over everyone in Him stands the settled verdict drawn from Romans 8: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1), for "God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do" (Romans 8:3). This is *sola gratia*, by grace alone, through *sola fide*, faith alone, in *solus Christus*, Christ alone: the way back is not a nearness you achieve — it is a nearness already bought, and you only have to come.

The word study for this series is the Greek word **hamartia** — to miss the mark: "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). Every missed mark separates, because every miss leaves us short of the God we were aimed for. That is why the remedy could never be better aim on our part. The One who never missed had to bring the far off near, and in His blood, He has.

John Owen (1616–1683), the Puritan pastor and author of *Communion with God*, spent his life teaching believers that fellowship with God is not a distant theory but the daily life of the soul — and that sin grieves and interrupts that communion even where it cannot destroy the union Christ has secured. Owen's counsel still fits Isaiah's diagnosis: do not make peace with the thing that makes you far. Run from the sin that hides His face, and run to the Christ whose blood has already brought you near.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — the "bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander" and "malice" Paul lists in Colossians 3:8, and every cherished sin that builds the wall higher. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): confess plainly, draw near today in prayer, and live as one already brought near — not as a stranger still outside the gate.

**Prayer:** LORD, my iniquities made the separation, and I could not cross it. Thank You that in Christ Jesus I who was far off have been brought near by His blood, and that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Him. Keep me from making peace with anything that hides Your face, and teach me to live today in the nearness You bought. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Why does God sometimes seem far off, according to Isaiah 59:2?
reflect.a: Not because His hand is shortened or His ear dull, but because "your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear" (Isaiah 59:2).

reflect.q: How are the far off brought near?
reflect.a: Not by climbing back, but by Christ's blood: "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ" (Ephesians 2:13).

reflect.q: What verdict stands over those brought near in Christ?
reflect.a: A settled one, in the present tense: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1).

devotionals.title: Love, Counted Slowly
body: Do not rush past the love chapter as if it were only wedding decoration. Paul wrote it to a gifted church in Corinth that was divided, impatient, and hungry for status, and he set it down as a mirror. Count it slowly, and let each line search you: “Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth. Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:4–7).

Count the bad news first, because Paul does. 1 — *Patient:* we are quick to snap. 2 — *Kind:* we can be correct and still be cold. 3 — *Does not envy:* we resent another's gift. 4 — *Does not boast, is not arrogant:* we use our gifts to be seen. 5 — *Not rude, does not insist on its own way:* we must win the room. 6 — *Not irritable or resentful:* we keep the record and replay it. 7 — *Does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth:* we are entertained by what should grieve us. Paul had already warned what all our religion amounts to without this love: “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1). Tongues, knowledge, generosity, even martyrdom — loud, impressive, and loveless — profit nothing. The law in this chapter exposes us: we have not loved like this for one full day.

Now count the good news, and read the same list again with Christ's name where Paul wrote love. Jesus is patient and kind. He does not envy or boast. He does not insist on His own way, though His way was heaven — in Gethsemane He prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). He bears all things, believes, hopes, and endures all things — enduring even the cross for sinners who had loved Him so poorly. And His love “never ends” (1 Corinthians 13:8). That is why the supply is not mere willpower: “God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). This is *sola gratia*, by grace alone, through *sola fide*, faith alone, in *solus Christus*, Christ alone: we do not climb into love to earn God; we receive God's love in Christ, and the Spirit then forms that same love, slowly and truly, in ordinary believers.

The word for love in this chapter is the Greek **agape** — committed, self-giving love that seeks the good of the other at cost to itself. Scripture uses the word with care, not as a slogan: the cross is its definition, for “by this we know love, that he laid down his life for us” (1 John 3:16). When Paul calls the church to agape, he is not calling us to a warmer feeling. He is calling us to the shape of Christ Himself, counted out in patience, kindness, and endurance toward real people.

Jonathan Edwards (1703–1758) preached a whole series on this chapter, later published as *Charity and Its Fruits*, arguing that love is not one grace among many but the sum and life of them all — the very fruit by which a true work of the Spirit is known. Edwards read 1 Corinthians 13 the way Paul wrote it: slowly, searching the heart, and driving the hearer away from mere gifts and noise toward Christ, who alone loves perfectly and who alone can make His people love.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which “belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires” (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — “bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander” and “malice” (Colossians 3:8), with envy, boasting, and the record of wrongs you keep rehearsing. *Put on* the new self, “created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (Ephesians 4:24), “which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:10): be patient with one slow person today, be kind where you could be cold, bear what you would rather drop, and endure in love because His love endures over you.

**Prayer:** LORD, I have counted Your Word and found my love wanting at every line. Thank You that Christ has loved perfectly in my place, and that You have poured Your love into my heart through the Holy Spirit. Make me patient and kind today, not insistent on my own way, quick to bear and slow to resent — and let the love I show point beyond me to Him. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Why did Paul write the love chapter to Corinth?
reflect.a: To a gifted but divided and status-hungry church, to show a “still more excellent way” (1 Corinthians 12:31) — that gifts without love are nothing: “but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1).

reflect.q: What does love do, counted from the text itself?
reflect.a: “Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful” (1 Corinthians 13:4–5), and “Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7).

reflect.q: Where does this love come from in the believer?
reflect.a: Not from willpower alone, but from God: “God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

devotionals.title: Great Is Thy Faithfulness
body: Dear friend,

I am writing to you this morning the way a pastor writes to someone sitting in the ashes — not with easy words, but with Jeremiah's words. And today, Veterans Day, I am thinking especially of those who served, who stood a watch, who waited in hard places and came home carrying what others never saw. Jeremiah knew something about holding a post in a ruined place. Lamentations is the Bible's book of tears: the prophet walking the smoking rubble of Jerusalem, everything he loved destroyed by the judgment he himself had predicted. If mercy only worked in comfort, it would have died there.

Hear the bad news first, because Jeremiah does not hide it. The city was gone, the temple was gone, and there was nothing in the rubble Jeremiah could point to and say, “At least this held.” Left to us, that is where the story ends — under judgment we have earned, with no strength left to rebuild what sin has broken. The law tells that truth plainly, and no morning, by itself, fixes it.

And it is *there*, sitting in the ashes, that Jeremiah speaks the most famous mercy-lines ever written: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23). He does not say God's mercies *might* return. He says they never came to an end in the first place. Then he makes it his own portion: “‘The LORD is my portion,’ says my soul, ‘therefore I will hope in him’” (Lamentations 3:24). Psalm 136 sings the same note twenty-six times over Israel's whole history — creation, Exodus, wilderness, conquest — and after every verse the answer comes back: “for his steadfast love endures forever.”

The Hebrew word underneath “steadfast love” is **hesed** — covenant love that will not let go, loyalty sworn by God and kept at cost to Himself. That one word carries this whole letter. Jeremiah's hope was not that he felt strong, or that the rubble had moved. His hope was *hesed*: the LORD had bound Himself to His people, and He would not unbind Himself in the ruins. In Christ that covenant love has a face and a cross. This is *sola gratia*, by grace alone, through *sola fide*, faith alone, in *solus Christus*, Christ alone: our portion is not a rebuilt city we hand to God — our portion is the LORD Himself, given to us in His Son, whose mercies reach us this morning before we did a single thing to earn them.

Thomas Chisholm (1866–1960) knew this faithfulness in an ordinary, unglamorous life. Frail in health and working low-paying jobs, with no dramatic rescue story to tell, he wrote in 1923 the hymn this verse became — “Great Is Thy Faithfulness” — testifying that over a whole lifetime, through strength for today and bright hope for tomorrow, God had never once failed to provide. Set to music by William Runyan, Jeremiah's ashes-confession became the song ordinary believers sing over ordinary faithfulness: not mercy in the miracle only, but mercy new every single morning.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which “belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires” (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — “anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth” (Colossians 3:8), with the despair that says the rubble is the end of the story. *Put on* the new self, “created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (Ephesians 4:24), “which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:10): wait quietly for the LORD today, receive this morning's mercy as this morning's portion, and thank one who served — not with a slogan, but by name.

**Prayer:** LORD, Your steadfast love never ceases, and Your mercies reached me new this morning before I earned a thing. Teach me, like Jeremiah, to hope in You from the ashes and not only from the comfort, and to call You my portion when everything else is gone. Bless those who served and who still carry the cost of it — be their portion too, and let them know Your faithfulness up close. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Where was Jeremiah when he wrote “great is your faithfulness”?
reflect.a: Not in comfort, but in the rubble of Jerusalem — and even there he confessed: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

reflect.q: What does Jeremiah call the LORD in the next verse?
reflect.a: His portion, and the ground of his hope: “‘The LORD is my portion,’ says my soul, ‘therefore I will hope in him’” (Lamentations 3:24).

reflect.q: How long does God's steadfast love endure, according to Psalm 136?
reflect.a: Forever — the refrain after every verse of Israel's story is: “for his steadfast love endures forever” (Psalm 136).

devotionals.title: Carmel: Twelve Stones and Four Jars of Water
body: Count it out, because Scripture counts it out. On Mount Carmel, the green ridge jutting into the Mediterranean, there were 450 prophets of Baal and 400 prophets of Asherah on one side (1 Kings 18:19), and on the other side one prophet of the LORD. Elijah said it plainly: “I, even I only, am a prophet of the LORD, but Baal's prophets are 450 men” (1 Kings 18:22). The numbers were not close, and they were never the point.

Hear the bad news first. Israel had not openly renounced the LORD — worse, she was trying to keep Him and Baal both. That is why Elijah's question cuts: “How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him” (1 Kings 18:21). Limping is our sin too: one foot with Christ on Sunday, one foot with the idols of comfort, money, and approval all week. The law exposes that split heart for what it is — no god at all can be served by halves, and a divided allegiance is already a decision against the LORD.

So Elijah rebuilt what sin had broken, and the specs matter. He “took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob” (1 Kings 18:31) — twelve, for a divided people God still counted as one. He dug a trench around the altar, he laid the wood and the bull in pieces, and then he made the miracle unmistakable: “Fill four jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and on the wood” — and do it a second time, and do it a third time (1 Kings 18:33–34). Four jars, three times: twelve jars of water, until “the water ran around the altar and filled the trench also with water” (1 Kings 18:35). No hidden spark, no dry tinder, no trick left to claim.

Then one short prayer, no shouting, no self-wounding such as Baal's prophets had done all day to silence: “Answer me, O LORD, answer me, that this people may know that you, O LORD, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back” (1 Kings 18:37). And the answer came by count as well: “Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the burnt offering and the wood and the stones and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench” (1 Kings 18:38). Five things consumed — offering, wood, stones, dust, and water — until nothing was left to doubt. “And when all the people saw it, they fell on their faces and said, ‘The LORD, he is God; the LORD, he is God’” (1 Kings 18:39).

The prophet's own name preaches the whole sermon. **Elijah** in Hebrew is *Eliyahu* — “My God is Yahweh,” *El*, God, joined to *Yahu*, the LORD's covenant name. Before Elijah ever prayed, his name declared the verdict Carmel proved: the LORD, and no other, is God. That is *solus Christus* and *soli Deo gloria* together — salvation and glory belong to the LORD alone, *sola gratia*, by grace alone, received *sola fide*, through faith alone. And Carmel points beyond itself: Christ ended all limping by His own once-for-all sacrifice, so no altar contest is ever needed again — God has answered finally, in His Son, and He turns hearts back to Himself.

Martin Luther stood in a Carmel-like place at Worms in 1521, outnumbered and pressed to take back what he had taught from Scripture, and he would not limp between two opinions; his conscience, he said, was captive to the Word of God. Carmel always comes down to that same ground: not numbers, not noise, but whether we will stand on God's Word when standing alone is the cost.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which “belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires” (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — “anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth” (Colossians 3:8), with the limping double life that tries to keep an idol on the side. *Put on* the new self, “created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (Ephesians 4:24), “which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:10): choose this day, plainly and wholly, and rebuild one broken altar in your life — one prayer, one obedience, left soaking wet with honesty before God.

**Prayer:** LORD, You are God, and there is no other. Forgive my limping between You and the idols I keep on the side, and turn my heart back the way You turned Israel's on Carmel. Let Your answer in Christ be enough for me today — no halves, no hiding. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: How many stones did Elijah use to rebuild the altar, and what did they stand for?
reflect.a: Twelve: he “took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob” (1 Kings 18:31) — a divided people God still counted as one.

reflect.q: What question did Elijah put to the people before the contest?
reflect.a: “How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him” (1 Kings 18:21).

reflect.q: What did the people cry when the fire fell?
reflect.a: They fell on their faces and said, “The LORD, he is God; the LORD, he is God” (1 Kings 18:39).

devotionals.title: Set My Feet Upon a Rock
body: David begins where every rescued man must begin: not with his own climbing, but with God's hearing. “I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry” (Psalm 40:1). Then comes the rescue itself, in one sentence that has carried men fighting to stay clean ever since: “He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure” (Psalm 40:2).

Hear the bad news first, because the psalm will not let us soften it. A pit is not a problem a man solves from inside it, and a miry bog gives no footing for a self-rescue. The teaching behind today's psalm names it plainly in song: a man digs his pit a little deeper every day, chasing what the darkness brings, until he has no strength left to even pray. That is the law's honest verdict on addiction, and on every sin that promises relief and delivers bondage. We do not slip once and recover by resolve. Left to ourselves, we sink, and the mud closes over our steps — we cannot make our own steps secure, because insecure steps are exactly the trouble.

The Hebrew word for that pit is *bor* — a cistern, a deep hole cut into rock, the kind of place Joseph was thrown into and Jeremiah was lowered into. A *bor* has no stairs. That one word preaches the whole doctrine: a man in a *bor* does not need advice, a ladder, or a stronger effort. He needs to be drawn up by a hand stronger than his own, from outside the pit. And that is precisely the verb David uses — not “I climbed,” but “He drew me up.”

Here is the good news, and it is all God's doing. The LORD inclined — He leaned down — and He heard, and He drew His servant up, and He did what the man could never do for himself: He set his feet upon a rock and made his steps secure. Then He finished the rescue with a gift no pit can produce: “He put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God. Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD” (Psalm 40:3). This is *sola gratia*, by grace alone, received *sola fide*, through faith alone, in *solus Christus*, Christ alone. Christ is the Rock on whom the Father sets the feet of everyone He draws out of sin's pit, and the security is His work, not ours — He makes the steps secure, and the rescued man's part is the new song, one day at a time.

John Newton (1725–1807) lived this psalm before he ever sang about it. A blaspheming sailor and slave trader, sunk in a life he later called a pit of his own digging, he cried out to God in a storm at sea in 1748 and was, by his own testimony, drawn up and set on new ground. The new song followed in due course — “Amazing Grace” — written by a man who never claimed he had climbed out, only that grace had found and carried him. David's song and Newton's tell the same story, because it is every believer's story.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which “belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires” (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — “anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth” (Colossians 3:8), with the old paths and old company that lead back toward the pit's edge. *Put on* the new self, “created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (Ephesians 4:24), “which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:10): stand today where He set you, one secure day at a time, and when the craving or the old lie comes knocking, cry out again to the God who has already shown He hears.

**Prayer:** LORD, I could not climb out, and You did not wait for me to try — You inclined to me, You heard my cry, and You drew me up. Keep my feet on the Rock today, make my steps secure, and keep the new song in my mouth when the old life calls me back. If You did it once, You will keep doing it, because the keeping is Yours. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: What did God do for David in Psalm 40:2?
reflect.a: He rescued him entirely: “He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure” (Psalm 40:2).

reflect.q: What came before the rescue in Psalm 40:1?
reflect.a: Waiting and a cry that God heard: “I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry” (Psalm 40:1).

reflect.q: What did God put in David's mouth after the rescue?
reflect.a: A witness that points others to trust Him: “He put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God. Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD” (Psalm 40:3).

devotionals.title: What Is the Trumpet Announcing?
body: What is a trumpet for, in Scripture? Not music for its own sake. A shofar — a trumpet made from a ram's horn, hollowed out, with no mouthpiece — was God's signal that He was announcing something no man could announce for himself. So ask the question Leviticus 25 forces us to ask: when that horn sounded through the whole land, what exactly was it announcing?

First, hear the bad news underneath it, because Jubilee only makes sense to debtors. By the fiftieth year, some in Israel owed debts they would never repay in a lifetime. Some had lost their family land — the inheritance God Himself had given them. Some had sold themselves into service because there was no other way to survive. The law is honest about this condition, and it will not let us pretend otherwise: a debtor cannot pay a debt by going deeper into debt, a slave cannot buy his own freedom, and lost ground does not come back by wishing. That is our picture in sin. We owe what we cannot pay, we have forfeited what God gave, and left to ourselves there is no fiftieth year coming by our own effort.

Now hear what the trumpet actually announced. God commanded: “Then you shall sound the loud trumpet on the tenth day of the seventh month. On the Day of Atonement you shall sound the trumpet throughout all your land. And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan” (Leviticus 25:9–10). Notice the order. The trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement — freedom was proclaimed only after atonement was made. Debts were cancelled, servants went free, and land returned, not because the debtors had finally earned it, but because God proclaimed liberty. That is *sola gratia*, by grace alone.

The Hebrew word behind “jubilee” is *yobel* — the ram's horn itself, and the blast of it. The year took its name from the instrument that announced it. In other words, Israel did not hear about freedom in a whisper or work it out in a ledger; they *heard* it, blown across the whole land, on God's authority. And this is the pattern of every shofar in Scripture: at Sinai “the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder” as God descended (Exodus 19:19), at Jericho the shofars blew and the walls fell (Joshua 6), and in Leviticus 25 the horn announced that freedom had come because God said it had come.

The good news is that Jesus took up this very announcement as His own first sermon. In the synagogue He read: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor” (Luke 4:18–19). The year of the Lord's favor is Jubilee language — and Christ did not merely announce it, He accomplished it at the cross, where the atonement the Day of Atonement pictured was made once for all. So Paul can say, “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery” (Galatians 5:1). *Solus Christus* — Christ alone sounds the trumpet over our lives, and what He proclaims, no debt and no devil can un-proclaim.

Martin Luther (1483–1546) understood this liberty in his bones. In *On the Freedom of a Christian* (1520), written as the Reformation was breaking open, he held the two truths together: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none — and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. Freedom in Christ is not freedom to drift back to the old master; it is freedom, bought by Another, that is gladly spent serving others. That is Jubilee lived out: released debtors do not return to the debtor's prison, they return to their inheritance and live as free men and women.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which “belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires” (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — “anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth” (Colossians 3:8), along with every old chain you are tempted to pick back up and call normal. *Put on* the new self, “created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (Ephesians 4:24), “which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:10): stand firm in the freedom Christ proclaimed over you today, and do not submit again to a yoke He has already broken.

**Prayer:** LORD, I could not pay what I owed, and I could not free myself — so You sounded the trumpet Yourself. Thank You that on the Day of Atonement's true fulfillment, in Christ, liberty was proclaimed to captives like me. Keep me standing firm in that freedom today, not running back to old chains, and let my free life serve others the way I have been served. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: When was the Jubilee trumpet sounded, and why does that timing matter?
reflect.a: On the Day of Atonement: “On the Day of Atonement you shall sound the trumpet throughout all your land” (Leviticus 25:9). Freedom was proclaimed only after atonement was made.

reflect.q: What did the trumpet proclaim in the fiftieth year?
reflect.a: Liberty for everyone in the land: “proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan” (Leviticus 25:10).

reflect.q: How does Jesus take up this announcement?
reflect.a: He proclaims it as His own mission: “to proclaim liberty to the captives… to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor” (Luke 4:18–19).

devotionals.title: Brought to the Desired Haven
devotionals.verse: Then they were glad that the waters were quiet, and he brought them to their desired haven
body: Psalm 107 is a psalm that teaches you how to respond. Four times it shows God's people in trouble, four times they cry out, and four times the same refrain returns: "Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress." The last picture is the sea — and it is the pattern of every shipwreck rescue in Scripture. Storm. Cry. Stillness. Haven. Read it slowly, and answer it as you go.

First, the storm — and hear the bad news honestly. "Some went down to the sea in ships, doing business on the great waters; they saw the deeds of the LORD, his wondrous works in the deep. For he commanded and raised the stormy wind, which lifted up the waves of the sea. They mounted up to heaven; they went down to the depths; their courage melted away in their evil plight; they reeled and staggered like drunken men and were at their wits' end" (Psalm 107:23–27). At their wits' end — that is the law's true work in us. Experienced sailors, men who knew the water for a living, had nothing left. No skill, no strength, no plan. That is where self-reliance ends for every one of us: not just wounded by sin, but unable to still a single wave of it. If we could reach the haven by our own rowing, we would not need a Deliverer.

Then the cry — and the good news that follows it. "Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed" (Psalm 107:28–29). Notice who does the work in those verses. They cried. He delivered. He made the storm be still. That is *sola gratia* — by grace alone — and *solus Christus*, Christ alone, for the One who stilled Psalm 107's sea later stood in a boat on Galilee, "rebuked the wind and said to the sea, 'Peace! Be still!' And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm" (Mark 4:39). The God who hushed the waves for crying sailors is the same Lord who hushes the storm of judgment for everyone who cries to Him in Christ. Our cry does not earn the calm; it receives it.

Then the haven — the verse to carry today: "Then they were glad that the waters were quiet, and he brought them to their desired haven" (Psalm 107:30). He brought them. Not "they finally found it," not "they drifted there by luck." The haven was desired — longed for through the whole storm — and it was given, because the bringing was God's work from first to last. And the psalm tells you how to respond when He brings you through: "Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man!" (Psalm 107:31). That steadfast love is the Hebrew word *hesed* — God's covenant love that does not let go, the love that holds when courage has melted and wits have run out. *Hesed* is why the anchor holds: "We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain" (Hebrews 6:19).

John Newton (1725–1807) knew this psalm in his body before he knew it in his head. A slave-ship sailor far from God, he was caught in a violent storm off Ireland on March 21, 1748, when the ship nearly went down and Newton — at his wits' end in the most literal sense — began to cry to the LORD for mercy. He marked that day for the rest of his life as the start of his conversion, and the man who had helped wreck so many lives spent his later years preaching the grace that had brought him to his desired haven — the grace he would put into the hymn "Amazing Grace." Newton's story is Psalm 107 with a name on it: the storm exposed him, the cry went up, and God did the bringing.

So respond to the psalm today the way it asks you to. If you are still in the storm, cry — that is not weakness, it is the psalm's own pattern. If He has hushed the waters for you, thank Him for His *hesed* by name. Either way, the order does not change, and neither does the One who brings His people home.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), along with the old habit of trusting your own rowing when the waves rise. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a man or woman who cries to the LORD first, thanks Him for His steadfast love, and trusts Him to do the bringing.

**Prayer:** LORD, I have been at my wits' end, and my courage has melted more than once — and every time, You were the One who stilled the storm and brought me through. Thank You for Your steadfast love, Your *hesed*, that never let go in the deep water. Teach me to cry to You first today, not last, and to thank You out loud when the waters grow quiet. Bring me, and everyone still out in the storm who is calling on You, to the haven You have desired for us. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: What is the pattern of rescue in Psalm 107:23–30?
reflect.a: Storm, cry, stillness, haven: the sailors were "at their wits' end" (v. 27), "then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress" (v. 28), "he made the storm be still" (v. 29), and "he brought them to their desired haven" (v. 30).

reflect.q: Who does the work of deliverance in this psalm?
reflect.a: God alone. The sailors' part was the cry; the delivering, the stilling, and the bringing were all His: "he delivered them from their distress. He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed" (Psalm 107:28–29).

reflect.q: How does the psalm say to respond once God has brought you through?
reflect.a: With thanksgiving for His covenant love: "Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man!" (Psalm 107:31).

devotionals.title: A Seat at the King's Table
devotionals.verse: So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet
body: Start with the hiding place, because that is where this story starts. Mephibosheth was the son of Jonathan and the grandson of King Saul — a surviving heir of the fallen dynasty David had replaced, and in that world surviving grandsons of dead kings did not live long. He was also lame, dropped by his nurse as a small boy while fleeing, "crippled in his feet" (2 Samuel 9:3), and living in Lo-debar — a name that means *no pasture, nothing*. Then the king sent for him. Hear the bad news honestly first: Mephibosheth had every reason, by the law of that world, to expect a sword, not a seat. He came expecting execution and fell on his face: "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?" (2 Samuel 9:8). That is what the law shows every one of us — crippled by the fall, belonging to a ruined house, with nothing to bring and nowhere to run.

Then hear what David actually said — and the good news in it. David had asked, "Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" (2 Samuel 9:1). And to the trembling man on the floor he said, "Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always" (2 Samuel 9:7). Notice whose name carries the whole gift. Not Mephibosheth's — Jonathan's. David did not do this because the lame man had earned it, asked for it, or could ever repay it. He did it because of a covenant made with someone else, long before. That kindness is the Hebrew word *chesed* — covenant love, steadfast kindness that keeps its promise because of who made the promise, not because of who receives it. So the last word on Mephibosheth is the anchor verse: "So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet" (2 Samuel 9:13). Both things stayed true at once — lame in both feet, and eating at the king's table always, "like one of the king's sons" (2 Samuel 9:11). At that table, nobody could see his lame feet. He was treated as a son because the covenant said so.

That is the gospel sitting at a table in the Old Testament, and it is *sola gratia* — by grace alone — from first to last. We are Mephibosheth: hiding from a King we assumed was our enemy, and God seats us at His table for Jesus's sake, because of a covenant we did not make and cannot keep. "But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved" (Ephesians 2:4–5). The seat is not a reward for learning to walk. It is a gift given to a man who never would.

Matthew Henry (1662–1714), the Puritan pastor whose commentary generations of believers have kept by their Bibles, lingered over this chapter as a picture of God's grace to sinners — a king seeking out a forgotten heir of a hostile house, not to judge him, but to feed him at his own table for another's sake. Henry's instinct is the church's instinct: read David's *chesed* here and you are meant to see a greater King, and a greater covenant, behind it.

So take your seat today without rehearsing why you do not deserve it — Mephibosheth already said that part, and the king answered it with a chair, not a lecture. The full teaching lives in the Grace series on the blog; today, just sit where grace has put you, and eat as a son or daughter, because the covenant says so.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), along with the old hiding — expecting judgment, calling yourself a dead dog, staying in Lo-debar when the King has sent for you. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a man or woman who comes when called, takes the seat given for Jesus's sake, and lives at the table as a child of the King.

**Prayer:** LORD, I came to You expecting judgment, and You gave me a seat at Your table — not for anything in me, but for Jesus's sake. Thank You for Your *chesed*, Your covenant kindness that sought me in a place of nothing and set me among Your sons and daughters. Teach me to stop hiding and stop rehearsing my unworthiness, and to live today at Your table in quiet confidence. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Why did David show kindness to Mephibosheth?
reflect.a: Not for anything Mephibosheth had done, but "for Jonathan's sake" (2 Samuel 9:1, 7) — because of a covenant made with his father long before.

reflect.q: What two things are true in the anchor verse at the same time?
reflect.a: "He ate always at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet" (2 Samuel 9:13). His lameness did not cancel his seat, and his seat did not depend on his healing.

reflect.q: How does this point to the gospel?
reflect.a: God seats sinners at His table for Jesus's sake, by grace alone: "even when we were dead in our trespasses, [He] made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved" (Ephesians 2:5).

devotionals.title: El Roi: The God Who Sees Me
devotionals.verse: So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, 'You are a God of seeing,' for she said, 'Truly here I have seen him who looks after me'
body: Stay with this one verse, phrase by phrase, because a runaway slave girl packed a whole theology into it. "So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, 'You are a God of seeing,' for she said, 'Truly here I have seen him who looks after me'" (Genesis 16:13).

First, *who* is speaking. Hagar was an Egyptian slave in Abram's household, pregnant with Ishmael, mistreated by Sarai, and now a runaway on the road to Shur — her road back to Egypt. She had no standing, no protector, and no reason to think anyone who mattered was looking for her. That is the bad news this verse refuses to skip: by every human measure, she was invisible. The people who should have cared for her had used her and driven her out. If her hope depended on being seen by people, she had none.

Second, *who found whom*. She did not climb up to God. The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, spoke to her, and gave her a promise over her unborn son. Then comes the wonder no one else in all of Scripture quite repeats: Abraham named a *place* for what God did (Genesis 22:14), and Moses named an *altar* (Exodus 17:15), but Hagar named *God Himself*. The name she gave Him is El Roi. The Hebrew word is *Ro'i* (pronounced roh-EE), from the verb *ra'ah*, "to see" — not a passing glance, but a seeing that looks after, that takes notice and cares. "You are a God of seeing... I have seen him who looks after me." The well itself kept the sermon: it was called Beer-lahai-roi, "the well of the Living One who sees me."

Third, *see how the seeing holds*. Years later Hagar was driven out a second time. The water ran out, and she laid her dying boy under a bush because she could not bear to watch. Then Scripture says, "God heard the voice of the boy" (Genesis 21:17) — just what the name Ishmael promised, "God hears" — and "God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water" (Genesis 21:19). The God who sees opened the eyes of the woman who had named Him for it. That is law then gospel in a wilderness: the law shows us our true condition — unseen, unheard, and unable to save ourselves or those we love — and the gospel answers that God Himself comes down the wilderness road, sees, hears, and provides. It is *sola gratia*, by grace alone. Hagar brought nothing but need. God brought everything else.

John Calvin (1509–1564), in his commentary on Genesis, taught the church to read accounts like this as more than ancient history — as a mirror of how God deals with His afflicted people still: He does not wait for the overlooked to make themselves noticeable, but stoops to meet them in their affliction. Generations of believers since have done what Hagar did — they gave God a name out of what He had done in their own wilderness, so they could preach it to themselves when the next dry spell came.

So name it today, plainly. You may be invisible to everyone who was supposed to care for you, but you are not unseen by God. You do not have to invent your hope; go back to your Beer-lahai-roi — the place where the Living One saw you — and drink again. The full teaching lives in the Hidden Gems collection on the blog; today, rest in this: the God who saw Hagar sees you, and in Christ He has looked after you for good.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), along with the old belief that if people overlook you, God has overlooked you too, and the running that belief drives. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a man or woman who stops running, returns where God sends, and lives today as one who is seen, heard, and looked after by the Living One.

**Prayer:** LORD, You are El Roi, the God who sees me. When I felt invisible and ran for the wilderness, You came looking — not because I climbed to You, but because You look after Your own. Thank You that in Christ You have seen my need and provided for it completely. Open my eyes today to the well You have already placed before me, and teach me to remember Your name when the road gets dry again. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
