reflect.q: What does El Roi mean, and who gave God this name?
reflect.a: Hagar, an Egyptian slave and runaway, named God El Roi — "You are a God of seeing" (Genesis 16:13). The Hebrew *Ro'i* comes from *ra'ah*, "to see" — a seeing that looks after and cares.

reflect.q: How do we know God's seeing was not a one-time glance?
reflect.a: Years later, when Hagar and Ishmael were dying of thirst, "God heard the voice of the boy" (Genesis 21:17) and "God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water" (Genesis 21:19). He saw, heard, and provided again.

reflect.q: What is the gospel in Hagar's story?
reflect.a: She brought only need, and God brought everything else — He found her, spoke to her, and provided for her by grace alone, a picture of how He seeks sinners in Christ rather than waiting for them to seek Him.

devotionals.title: By His Wounds
devotionals.verse: But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed
body: Seven hundred years before the cross, Isaiah sang a song no one wanted to hear. It is the fourth of his Servant Songs (Isaiah 52:13–53:12), and its center stands plain: "But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5).

Read it slowly, in classic order — bad news first, then good news, because the song itself refuses to skip either. The bad news is in the little word *our*. He was pierced for *our* transgressions, crushed for *our* iniquities. The Servant had committed neither. Isaiah had already named Him "a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3), despised and rejected, silent before His accusers "like a lamb that is led to the slaughter" (Isaiah 53:7), cut off from the land of the living and assigned a grave "with the wicked and with a rich man in his death" (Isaiah 53:9). None of that suffering was payment for His own sin, for He had none. That is the law doing its honest work: it shows us that the wounds were not an accident of history and not a debt He owed — they were ours, transferred.

The good news is the exchange itself — substitution, written in advance. Upon Him was the chastisement that brought us peace. The Hebrew word for that discipline is *musar* — the corrective punishment a guilty person has earned — and the peace it purchased is *shalom*, wholeness, being made right and whole with God. He took the *musar*; we receive the *shalom*. He was wounded; we are healed. That is *sola gratia* and *sola fide* together: by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone — not by our wounds, our penance, or our improvement, but by His wounds in our place.

The New Testament will not let this stay as prophecy only. An Ethiopian official was reading this very chapter in his chariot when Philip climbed up and, beginning with this Scripture, "told him the good news about Jesus" (Acts 8:35). Peter preached the same song to the church: "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree... By his wounds you have been healed" (1 Peter 2:24). Your healing and your peace are not wishes. They were purchased, and the receipt was written seven centuries before Calvary.

John Calvin (1509–1564), in his commentary on Isaiah, pressed this chapter on his readers as the clearest Old Testament picture of Christ's substitution — that the Servant stood in the place of sinners so completely that believers can read their own transgressions in His piercing and their own peace in His chastisement. Generations of Reformers and Puritans after him kept returning to Isaiah 53 for the same reason: when conscience accuses, this song answers with a finished exchange, not a probationary one.

So rest in it today, plainly. If your peace depended on how well you have healed yourself, you would have none. It depends on wounds that are not yours, borne by a Servant who, after suffering, would "see his offspring" and "prolong his days" (Isaiah 53:10) because He had borne "the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12). The risen Christ is the proof the exchange held. The full teaching lives in The Prophetic Series on the blog; today, stand on this: by His wounds, you are healed.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), along with the old habit of trying to pay for your own peace with guilt, penance, and self-punishment. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a man or woman who brings transgressions to the pierced Servant, receives His peace, and lives today healed — not half-forgiven and still on trial, but at peace with God through Christ.

**Prayer:** LORD, Your Servant was pierced for my transgressions and crushed for my iniquities, and the chastisement that brought me peace fell on Him. Thank You that my healing was purchased by His wounds and not by my own striving. Teach me to stop trying to pay what He has already paid, and to live today in the *shalom* He bought — whole, forgiven, and at peace with You. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Whose transgressions was the Servant pierced for?
reflect.a: Ours. "He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities" (Isaiah 53:5). The Servant had no sin of His own to pay for.

reflect.q: What do the Hebrew words *musar* and *shalom* show us in this verse?
reflect.a: *Musar* is the corrective chastisement the guilty had earned, and *shalom* is the peace and wholeness it brought. He took the *musar*; we receive the *shalom*.

reflect.q: How did the New Testament use this chapter?
reflect.a: Philip used it to tell the Ethiopian official "the good news about Jesus" (Acts 8:35), and Peter applied it directly to the church: "By his wounds you have been healed" (1 Peter 2:24).

devotionals.title: Why Do We Run From the Throne We Need?
devotionals.verse: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need
body: Why do we run from the very throne we need? That is the question Hebrews 4 asks of every sinner who knows his need and still stays away. The writer does not begin with our running — he begins with our High Priest: "For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). And then comes the boldest invitation in all of Scripture: "Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need" (Hebrews 4:16).

Read it in classic order — bad news first, then good news, because the question itself demands both. The bad news is why we run at all. Guilt tells us the throne is a throne of judgment, and judgment is what we deserve. Sin has taught us to hide — Adam hid among the trees, Israel trembled at the mountain and begged Moses to speak for them, and the prodigal rehearsed his speech for the road home, certain he would be hired help at best. The law has done its honest work: it has shown us that we have no claim, no merit, and no clean record to present. So we keep our distance. We pray small prayers at arm's length, we promise to come back when we are cleaner, and we call that reverence. It is not reverence. It is unbelief wearing a religious coat.

The good news answers the question itself. Why do we run from the throne we need? Because we have mistaken what kind of throne it is. Hebrews does not call it the throne of judgment. It calls it the throne of *grace*. The doorkeeper is not a stranger to our weakness — He was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin, and He sympathizes with us from the inside. And the invitation is not "crawl," not "wait to be summoned," not "come when you have fixed yourself." It is "draw near with confidence." The Greek word is *parrēsia* — boldness, free and open speech, the liberty of a child who belongs in the room. That boldness is not in ourselves; it is in our Priest. We do not bring our worthiness to the throne. We bring our need, and the throne gives us two named gifts: mercy for what is past, and grace for the need that is present — "in time of need" means bring the need while it is still a need.

That is *solus Christus* and *sola gratia* together: through Christ alone, by grace alone, the throne of the universe is open for mercy business right now. And mercy received does not stay received. Jude turns the receiver into a rescuer: "And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire" (Jude 22-23). The people of God are not a museum of the forgiven; we are a rescue crew of the merciful — snatching others because we know exactly Who snatched us. Run to the throne boldly, and then run back out to the roadside, the ditch, and the far country with the same cry answered in your own voice: the Lord delights in mercy — come and see.

John Calvin (1509–1564), commenting on Hebrews 4:16, pressed this same point on his readers: our confidence in approaching God does not rest on anything in ourselves, but on Christ our High Priest, who has opened the way and stands before the Father for us. Calvin warned that to shrink back from the throne is to act as though Christ had not done His work — and to draw near boldly is simply to believe what God has already said about His Son. The Reformers kept returning to this verse for the same reason: when conscience says "stay away," the throne of grace says "come."

So come today, plainly. Bring the need as it is. Plead nothing but His character, and receive mercy multiplied — "May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you" (Jude 2). The full teaching lives in the Mercy series on the blog; today, stop running from the throne you need, and run to it.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), along with the old habit of hiding from God until you feel worthy enough to pray. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): a man or woman who draws near with *parrēsia* — bold, free speech before the throne of grace — receiving mercy for the past and grace for the present need, and then carrying that same mercy out to someone still running.

**Prayer:** LORD, I have run from the throne I need, hiding behind my guilt and calling it reverence. Thank You for a High Priest who sympathizes with my weakness, who was tempted as I am yet without sin, and who bids me come with confidence. Give me *parrēsia* — boldness not in myself, but in Him. Let me receive mercy for what is past and find grace for the need I carry today, and make me a rescuer of others the way You rescued me. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Why does Hebrews say we can draw near to the throne with confidence?
reflect.a: Because our High Priest sympathizes with our weaknesses — He "has been tempted as we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). Our confidence rests on Him, not on our own worthiness.

reflect.q: What does the Greek word *parrēsia* mean in Hebrews 4:16?
reflect.a: Boldness — free and open speech, the liberty of a child who belongs in the room. We approach the throne of grace boldly because Christ has opened the way.

reflect.q: What two gifts does the throne of grace give us?
reflect.a: Mercy for the past and grace for the present need: "that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need" (Hebrews 4:16) — and Jude shows mercy received becomes mercy given, snatching others out of the fire (Jude 22-23).

devotionals.title: Joy — Chara
devotionals.verse: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness
body: Paul puts joy second in the harvest, and he puts it there on purpose: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness" (Galatians 5:22). Count joy the way this list asks to be counted — slowly, honestly, and in order — because joy in Scripture is not the world's happiness wearing church clothes.

Count the bad news first. 1 — *Our happiness takes its orders from circumstances:* when the provision holds, we sing; when it fails, we sink, as if God had changed with the weather. 2 — *Envy steals what joy remains:* envy, joy's exact opposite, cannot rejoice at another's blessing, because it measures everything against the self and grieves when a brother is honored. 3 — *We try to manufacture gladness by willpower:* we paste on cheerfulness, deny the pain, and call it faith — and it cracks by noon. The law tells the truth about all three: left to the flesh, we are sorrowful without the "yet" — we have grief about what is happening and nothing underneath it about what is true.

Now count the good news, in the same order. 1 — *Joy rests on something solid:* the Greek word is *chara* (χαρά) — gladness, deep delight, a rejoicing that rests on something solid. It is kin to *charis*, grace: joy is what grace feels like when it is received and believed. It belongs to the kingdom itself: "For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Romans 14:17). 2 — *Joy and grief can occupy the same heart:* Paul calls himself "sorrowful, yet always rejoicing" (2 Corinthians 6:10), because grief is about what is happening, and joy is about what is true — reconciled to God, forgiven, adopted, kept, and heaven-bound. Habakkuk watched every visible provision fail at once and still resolved: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation" (Habakkuk 3:18). 3 — *Joy has a face, and it is Christ's:* "In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit" (Luke 10:21); He spoke so "that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full" (John 15:11); and He went to the cross "for the joy that was set before him" (Hebrews 12:2) — the joy located not in the suffering itself, but beyond it. That is *sola gratia* and *solus Christus* together: joy is not a temperament we bring to God, but a fruit the Spirit grows in people who belong to Jesus.

So how does it grow? By looking at the right things on purpose. It is commanded — "Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice" (Philippians 4:4), written from prison — not because feelings obey orders, but because the attention that feeds joy does. Count mercies by name. Sing when the heart is heavy. Rehearse the gospel's facts until the feelings catch up with the facts. And stay at the table with God's people, whose gladness is contagious in a way isolation never is: "The joy of the LORD is your strength" (Nehemiah 8:10). The full teaching lives in the Fruit of the Spirit series on the blog; today, count joy slowly — and let the counting itself become rejoicing.

Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834–1892), who knew deep and recurring depression across his ministry, refused to treat joy as a matter of temperament or a prize for the naturally cheerful. He kept preaching joy as the believer's duty and gift at once — a gladness that rests not on how the day feels, but on who the Lord is and what He has done in Christ. Spurgeon is a fitting witness for this fruit: a sorrowful man who was, in Paul's words, always rejoicing, because his joy was stored where his sorrows could not reach it.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), along with envy that grieves at another's blessing and the circumstance-ruled despair that calls sinking honesty. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): count three specific mercies by name today, thank God for each out loud, and rejoice over one specific blessing in somebody else's life — and tell them so.

**Prayer:** LORD, my gladness has taken its orders from my circumstances for too long, and envy has stolen what was left. Thank You that joy is Your fruit, not my temperament — *chara*, the gladness of grace received and believed, grown by Your Spirit in those who belong to Christ. Teach me to be sorrowful, yet always rejoicing: to count Your mercies by name, to rehearse what is true until my feelings catch up, and to rejoice at my brother's blessing as gladly as my own. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: What has failed in Habakkuk's life when he says "yet I will rejoice"?
reflect.a: Everything visible: the fig tree, the vines, the olive, the fields, the flock, and the herd (Habakkuk 3:17). His "yet" does not rest on provision returning — it rests on the God of his salvation: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation" (Habakkuk 3:18).

reflect.q: How can joy and the cross stand in one sentence in Hebrews 12:2?
reflect.a: Because the joy was not in the suffering itself, but beyond it — set before Christ on the far side of it: He "for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame" (Hebrews 12:2).

reflect.q: What is the one specific thing to do with this today?
reflect.a: Write down three specific mercies of God to you — not general ones — and thank Him for each out loud. Then rejoice over one specific blessing in somebody else's life, and tell them so.

devotionals.title: 450 Feet of Obedience
devotionals.verse: This is how you are to make it: the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits
body: God did not give Noah a feeling. He gave him measurements: "This is how you are to make it: the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits" (Genesis 6:15). At roughly eighteen inches to the cubit, count the specs the way Scripture gives them. **300 long, 50 wide, 30 high** — about 450 feet by 75 feet by 45 feet, a vessel longer than a football field. **Three decks** — "Make it with lower, second, and third decks" — **one roof** finished to a cubit above, **one door** set in its side, rooms throughout, and pitch covering it "inside and out" (Genesis 6:14, 16). Before there was a wreck anywhere in Scripture, there was this: a rescue ship built to God's numbers, by a man who had never seen rain, far from any sea.

Count the bad news first, because the specs only make sense against it. The world Noah built in was not neutral ground: "The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5). Judgment was not a possibility; it was announced. And Noah had nothing in himself to stand on — no righteousness of his own manufacture, no ark of his own design. Left to ourselves, that is still the count: a flood of judgment we cannot outswim, and hands that cannot build their way to God. That is the law's honest arithmetic, and it adds up to zero for us.

Now count the good news in the same numbers. **One word of grace comes before one board is cut:** "But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD" (Genesis 6:8) — favor first, building second; that is *sola gratia* in Genesis. **Eight persons** were carried through: Peter says that in the ark "a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water" (1 Peter 3:20) — judgment all around the vessel, and every soul inside it saved. **One door** — and God set it, and in the end God shut it. And **one act of faith** ran through every cubit: "Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him" (Genesis 6:22). Hebrews names what the measuring and hammering really were: "By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household" (Hebrews 11:7). The Hebrew word for the vessel is *tevah* (תֵּבָה) — used in all of Scripture only for Noah's ark and for the little basket that carried Moses through the water (Exodus 2:3). Twice God puts His saving purpose in a *tevah*, and twice everyone inside comes through. The ark is a picture ahead of its time of *solus Christus*: salvation is not found by the strong swimmer, but by being in the vessel God provided.

John Calvin, commenting on Genesis, lingered on exactly this — that Noah obeyed a command that looked foolish to the age around him, building for a judgment no eye could yet see, and that his obedience was faith taking God at His word before there was any evidence to point to. That is still how faith builds: not because the sky looks threatening, but because God has spoken. The full teaching lives in the Shipwrecked series on the blog; today, take God at His word at the size He gave it — 450 feet of obedience started with believing Him about the first cubit.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), along with the unbelief that will not move until it can see the rain. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): take one plain command of God you have been postponing, and obey it today at full measure — not a token cubit, the whole length.

**Prayer:** LORD, You saved Noah by grace before he lifted a tool, and You carried all eight souls through in the vessel You designed. I cannot outswim judgment and I cannot build my way to You — thank You that salvation is being in Christ, the vessel You provided. Give me Noah's kind of faith: to take You at Your word about things as yet unseen, and to obey at full measure. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: What are the ark's God-given dimensions, and what do they come to in feet?
reflect.a: "The length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits" (Genesis 6:15) — at roughly eighteen inches to the cubit, about 450 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high, with lower, second, and third decks (Genesis 6:16).

reflect.q: What came first for Noah — grace, or building?
reflect.a: Grace. "But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD" (Genesis 6:8) is spoken before the building begins, and Hebrews says the building itself was faith: Noah "in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household" (Hebrews 11:7).

reflect.q: What is the one specific thing to do with this today?
reflect.a: Name one plain command of God you have been postponing, and obey it today at full measure — the whole length, not a token part of it.

devotionals.title: Still in the Potter's Hand
devotionals.verse: O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter has done? declares the LORD. Behold, like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel
body: Dear friend,

If you feel marred today — cracked by your own sin, by years you cannot get back, by a life that did not turn out the shape you prayed for — I am writing to you from a potter's house in Jeremiah's day, because God sent His prophet there on purpose to watch clay fail and be remade.

God told Jeremiah to go down and look. "And the vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do" (Jeremiah 18:4). Then God applied it Himself, and this is the anchor for today: "O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter has done? declares the LORD. Behold, like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel" (Jeremiah 18:6).

Hear the bad news first, plainly, because a pastoral word that skips it helps no one. The vessel really was spoiled. Scripture does not call the marring an illusion, and it does not blame the wheel. We are clay that resists the hand — we want our own shape, our own cisterns, our own way — and apart from grace we stay marred. Left to ourselves we cannot rework ourselves into another vessel; a lump of clay has never once thrown itself. That is the law's honest word, and it humbles every one of us.

Now hear the good news in the very same scene, and notice where everything happens. The vessel was spoiled *in the potter's hand* — and it was reworked *in the potter's hand*. He did not sweep it off the wheel. He did not throw it in the scrap pile. He reworked it, as it seemed good to *him* to do. Your hope is not that you were never marred; your hope is whose hand you are in. This is *sola gratia* at a potter's wheel: the remaking is the Potter's work, from first touch to finished vessel.

It has been this way since the beginning. When Genesis says God made man, the Hebrew word is *yatsar* — "then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground" (Genesis 2:7). *Yatsar* is the potter's word, to fashion clay by hand, and the potter in Jeremiah's house is a *yotser*, from that same root. You were not manufactured and forgotten. You were formed by hand, and the hand that formed you has not let go. Isaiah prayed this truth back to God for a whole people who felt ruined: "But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand" (Isaiah 64:8).

John Calvin, writing on Jeremiah, pressed this comfort home: God's people are not in the grip of chance or of their own ruined past, but in the hand of the One who governs all things for their good — the same hand that permits the marring to be seen is the hand that remakes. The warning of Jeremiah 19 stands beside it in the teaching, and it is not God's mood that changes between the chapters; it is the clay's posture. The vessel of chapter 18 stayed on the wheel and was remade. Brokenness brought to the Potter is the beginning of remaking. So stay on the wheel, friend. The full teaching lives in the Broken Vessels series on the blog; today, rest in this one sentence — marred in the hand, remade in the hand, never out of the hand.

**Put off / put on:** *Put off* the old self, which "belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22), and put away what belongs to it — "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), along with the despair that calls yourself scrap. *Put on* the new self, "created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:24), "which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10): name one marred place in your life today, and instead of hiding it or hardening against God over it, bring it honestly to Him in prayer and stay under His hand.

**Prayer:** Father, we are the clay and You are our Potter; we are all the work of Your hand. I confess I cannot remake myself, and I thank You that in Christ You have not thrown this vessel away. Keep me on Your wheel, soften what has hardened, and rework me as it seems good to You. Soli Deo Gloria. In Jesus' name, amen.
*Meeting others where they are in the Name of Jesus* Christ Proclaimed. Jesus is Lord.

reflect.q: Where was the vessel when it was spoiled, and where was it when it was remade?
reflect.a: In the potter's hand both times: "the vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do" (Jeremiah 18:4).

reflect.q: What does God Himself say this picture means?
reflect.a: "Behold, like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel" (Jeremiah 18:6) — His people are held and reworked by Him, not discarded by Him.

reflect.q: What is the one specific thing to do with this today?
reflect.a: Name one marred place in your life, bring it honestly to God in prayer, and stay under His hand instead of hiding it or hardening over it.

weeklyStudies.title: Arrest the Thought, Fill the Mind

days.title: The Battlefield
days.focus: The fight is real, but it is not fought with fleshly weapons. The strongholds are thoughts — arguments and lofty opinions raised against the knowledge of God. A stronghold is a lie believed so long it feels like a fact.
days.question: What is one stronghold-thought that has dug in over the years — and can you say it plainly, in one sentence?

days.title: The Standard
days.focus: Every thought is measured against one standard: what God has said. "Your word is truth." The Word stored in the heart is the weapon already in the house when the fight comes — you cannot arrest a lie with a verse you do not have.
days.question: Which verse do you actually have stored up right now that answers your stronghold from Day 1?

days.title: The Exchange
days.focus: Before Paul ever lists what to think on, he gives the trade: anxiety out, prayer in — and the peace of God stands guard over heart and mind in Christ Jesus. The guard is posted by prayer. The mind does its work under His protection, not alone.
days.question: What is the specific anxiety you will trade in prayer today — named, not general?

days.title: The Filling, Part 1
days.focus: TRUE — what matches reality as God sees it. HONORABLE — what carries weight and dignity. JUST — what is right and fair by God's standard. PURE — what could be brought into the light without shame. The arrested thought leaves ground behind; these four are the first stones of the rebuilding.
days.question: Of the four, which replacement thought do you most need today — and what is it, in your own words?

days.title: The Filling, Part 2
days.focus: LOVELY — what calls forth love and softens the heart. COMMENDABLE — what would be a credit if said out loud. EXCELLENCE — not barely-allowed, but the best. WORTHY OF PRAISE — what God Himself would applaud. The standard rises from "not sinful" to "worthy of Him."
days.question: What have you been dwelling on lately that passes "not sinful" but fails "excellent"?

days.title: The Person Behind the List
days.focus: The eight qualities are not eight chores — they are one Christ, seen from eight sides. He is the Truth. He is just and pure. He is altogether lovely. "Think about these things" finally means fix your eyes on Him and set your mind on things above, where He is.
days.question: When you picture fixing your eyes on Jesus (Hebrews 12:2), which of the eight qualities do you see in Him most clearly — and why that one?

days.title: The Deep Dive and the Week's Reflection
days.read: "Arrest the Thought, Fill the Mind" (the full deep-dive study), slowly, with a pen.

reflect.q: What is a stronghold, and what does God say to do with it?
reflect.a: A stronghold is a thought dug in against the knowledge of God — a lie believed so long it feels like a fact. It is not to be negotiated with or managed; by the weapons God gives, it is destroyed, and every thought is taken captive to obey Christ (2 Corinthians 10:4–5).

reflect.q: Why must the arrested thought be replaced, and not just removed?
reflect.a: Because a mind is never empty. Paul pairs the two movements on purpose: arrest what opposes God (2 Corinthians 10:5), then dwell on what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, excellent, and worthy of praise (Philippians 4:8). Victory is replacement — Christ in the place the lie stood.

reflect.q: Where does peace come from in this fight — my effort, or somewhere else?
reflect.a: From God, through prayer. "Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:6–7). I bring the requests; He posts the guard.

reflect.q: What standard decides if a thought may stay?
reflect.a: The knowledge of God — what He has said in His Word, which is truth (John 17:17). Feelings do not get a vote; circumstances do not get the final word. A thought that agrees with God's Word may stay. A thought that opposes it is a captive to take.

reflect.q: Who is the filling, finally — a list, or a Person?
reflect.a: A Person. All eight qualities are perfectly true of Jesus Christ: He is the Truth (John 14:6), the Righteous One (1 John 2:1), unstained and pure (Hebrews 7:26), altogether lovely (Song of Solomon 5:16). To think on these things is to fix your eyes on Him (Hebrews 12:2) — and the same hands that were nailed to the cross are the hands holding the mind that trusts Him. **Closing prayer for the week:** Lord, teach me the whole motion — to arrest every thought that rises against Your Word, and to fill my mind with Your Son. Guard my heart and my mind in Christ Jesus, and let what I dwell on this week make me more like Him. Amen. --- *Prepared for Lewis Fuller. Companion pieces: "Philippians 4:8 — Think on These Things" (the eight qualities one by one) and "Arrest the Thought, Fill the Mind" (the deep dive). Memory verses in the same fight: 2 Corinthians 10:5 (Week 1), Philippians 4:8 (Week 3, beginning Monday, November 23, 2026), Psalm 119:11 (Week 5), Hebrews 12:2 (Week 7).*

weeklyStudies.title: Live Like You Belong to Him

days.title: The Wardrobe
days.focus: Before Paul names a single garment, he names who is wearing them: "God's chosen ones, holy and beloved." The clothing follows the identity — you dress like who you already are in Christ, not to become someone else. The first five pieces: compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience.
days.question: Which of the five do you most often leave hanging in the closet — and what would today look like with it on?

days.title: Bear and Forgive
days.focus: "Bearing with one another" comes before forgiving — some days you simply carry a person you cannot fix. And when there is a real complaint, the pattern is not their apology; it is His pardon: "as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive." Forgiveness runs downhill from the cross.
days.question: Is there someone you are still waiting on to make the first move — and what does "as the Lord has forgiven you" say to that wait?

days.title: Above All, Love
days.focus: Love is not one more item on the list; it is the garment over all the others, "which binds everything together in perfect harmony." Without it, patience turns cold, kindness turns mechanical, and forgiveness turns into bookkeeping. With it, the whole outfit holds together.
days.question: Which virtue from this week is hardest for you to wear toward the people closest to you — and what would love over it change?

days.title: Let Peace Rule
days.focus: The word Paul uses for "rule" pictures an umpire — the one who makes the call. The peace of Christ is not a feeling to chase; it is a referee to obey. When anxiety and peace argue in the same heart, peace gets the whistle — because we were "called in one body" to it. And the verse ends with the discipline underneath it all: "And be thankful."
days.question: Where is a dispute going on in your heart right now — and have you let peace make the call, or is anxiety still holding the whistle?

days.title: The Word Dwelling In
days.focus: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly." Not visit. Not pass through. Dwell — live there, richly, with room to spare. A heart where the Word only visits is a heart furnished by whatever else moved in. This is the same fight as the memory verses: what dwells in you is what comes out of you — teaching, admonishing, even singing.
days.question: If your heart were a house, what has actually been dwelling in it this week — and what would "richly" add?

days.title: Sing, and Do All in His Name
days.focus: The passage ends wide open: singing with thankfulness, and then everything — "whatever you do, in word or deed" — done in the name of the Lord Jesus. No corner of the day is left secular. The smallest task, done in His name and with thanks, is worn as worship.
days.question: What is one ordinary thing on today's list you have never once done "in the name of the Lord Jesus" on purpose — and what changes if you do?

days.title: The Full Piece and the Week's Reflection
days.read: "Live Like You Belong to Him" (the full piece, below), slowly, with a pen.

reflect.q: Who does Paul say you are before he tells you what to put on — and why does the order matter?
reflect.a: "God's chosen ones, holy and beloved" (Colossians 3:12). The order is everything: the clothing follows the identity. We do not dress this way to become God's; we dress this way because we already are His in Christ. Backwards, it is performance. In order, it is a son wearing his Father's likeness.

reflect.q: What sets the measure for forgiving someone who has wronged you?
reflect.a: Not their apology, and not your feelings — His pardon: "as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive" (Colossians 3:13). He forgave first, fully, at the cost of the cross. Forgiveness that waits to be earned is not the kind we received, so it cannot be the kind we give.

reflect.q: What does love do that the other virtues cannot do alone?
reflect.a: It binds them. "Above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony" (Colossians 3:14). Patience without love turns cold; kindness without love turns mechanical; forgiveness without love turns into bookkeeping. Love is the garment over all the others that holds the whole outfit together.

reflect.q: What does it mean for the peace of Christ to "rule" in your heart?
reflect.a: The word pictures an umpire — the one who makes the call. "Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful" (Colossians 3:15). Peace is not a mood to wait for; it is an authority to yield to. When fear and faith argue, peace holds the whistle.

reflect.q: How much of the day does verse 17 actually cover?
reflect.a: All of it. "Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him" (Colossians 3:17). No secular corner, no off-duty hour. The smallest task done in His name, with thanks, is worn as worship by a man who belongs to Him. **Closing prayer for the week:** Lord, You have not left me in the grave clothes. You chose me, made me holy, called me beloved — now teach me to dress like it. Put compassion on my heart, forgiveness on my lips, love over it all, and let Your peace make the calls in me. Whatever I do this week, let it be done in the name of the Lord Jesus, with thanks. Amen. --- *Prepared for Lewis Fuller. Companion thread: the nightly put off / put on posts on his personal profile walk this same chapter pair by pair. Source passage suggested by a Linda Seidler Daily video Lewis shared November 19, 2026 ("Live like you belong to Him" — Colossians 3:12–17).*

weeklyStudies.title: Don't Let Worry Have the Final Word

days.title: The Ground
days.focus: "Do not be anxious about anything" does not stand alone — the verse before it gives the reason: "The Lord is at hand." This is not a scolding for feeling weak. It is an invitation built on a nearness: you are not carrying this alone, because He is not far off. The command rests on the presence.
days.question: What is the worry you have been carrying as if the Lord were far away — and what changes if He is at hand, right here?

days.title: Pray About Everything
days.focus: Paul's answer to anxiety is not "think harder" or "calm down" — it is a trade: "in everything by prayer and supplication." Everything means everything. The big diagnosis and the small bill. Nothing is too large for His power or too small for His care. Worry talks to itself; prayer talks to God. Only one of those conversations can change anything.
days.question: What is one thing you have only worried about so far and never actually prayed about — and will you bring it today?

days.title: Tell God What You Need
days.focus: "Let your requests be made known to God." He already knows — the telling is for us. Vague dread stays heavy; a named request can be carried. God is not honored by our pretending we need nothing. He is honored when His children ask plainly, like children, for what they actually need.
days.question: If you had to say your need in one honest sentence — no dressing it up — what would it be?

days.title: With Thanksgiving
days.focus: Thanksgiving is not the garnish on prayer; Paul puts it inside the asking: "by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving." While you ask for what you need next, you remember what He has already done. Gratitude is memory with its eyes open — and it changes the voice of the prayer from panic to trust.
days.question: Name three things He has already done for you that you can thank Him for in the same breath as today's request.

days.title: The Peace That Guards
days.focus: The promise is not that we manufacture calm — it is that "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds." The word for guard, *phroureō*, is a soldier's word: to stand garrison, to keep watch over a city. God's peace is not a mood that comes and goes; it is a sentry He posts. We bring the requests; He posts the guard.
days.question: Where do you most need a guard posted tonight — over your heart (what you feel) or your mind (what you rehearse)?

days.title: Hearts and Minds in Christ Jesus
days.focus: Notice where the guard stands: "in Christ Jesus." The peace is not located in the circumstances turning out right — it is located in a Person. That is why it can surpass understanding: it holds even when nothing around us makes sense yet. The heart and the mind — the two fronts of every anxious war — are both covered, both in Him.
days.question: What circumstance have you been waiting to change before you let yourself have peace — and what if the peace is in Christ, not in the circumstance?

days.title: The Full Piece and the Week's Reflection
days.read: "Don't Let Worry Have the Final Word" (the full piece, below), slowly, with a pen.

reflect.q: Is "do not be anxious" just a command to try harder not to feel afraid?
reflect.a: No. The command stands on a ground and comes with a trade. The ground: "The Lord is at hand" (Philippians 4:5). The trade: "in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God" (Philippians 4:6). God does not leave us with a bare command and our feelings — He gives us His nearness and something to do with the worry: hand it over in prayer.

reflect.q: What are we supposed to do with a worry — suppress it, or something else?
reflect.a: Trade it. Worry is rehearsing the need to yourself; prayer is presenting the need to God. Paul's pattern is specific: pray about everything, make your requests known plainly, and do it with thanksgiving (Philippians 4:6). A named request can be carried by God. Vague dread just sits on our own chest.

reflect.q: Why does Paul put thanksgiving inside the asking, before the answer comes?
reflect.a: Because thanksgiving is memory at work. While we ask for what we need next, we remember what He has already done — and the God who carried us then is the God we are asking now. Gratitude does not deny the need; it steadies the voice of the prayer from panic to trust (Philippians 4:6).

reflect.q: What is the peace of God, and what does it actually do?
reflect.a: It is God's own peace, and it stands guard: "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:7). The word for guard is a garrison word — a sentry posted at a gate. We do not manufacture this peace or hold onto it by effort; God posts it, and it holds.

reflect.q: Why can this peace hold even when the circumstances have not changed?
reflect.a: Because of where it is posted: "in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:7). Peace located in circumstances lasts only as long as the circumstances behave. Peace located in a Person — the Lord who is at hand — holds in the middle of the unknown, which is exactly where it is needed most. **Closing prayer for the week:** Lord, You are at hand — nearer than the worry that has been talking so loud. I bring You my requests now, plainly, and I thank You for all You have already done. Post Your peace as the guard over my heart and my mind in Christ Jesus, and let worry speak its piece — but never the final word. That word is Yours. Amen. --- *Prepared for Lewis Fuller. Companion pieces: "Arrest the Thought, Fill the Mind" (Week 1, Nov 23 — its Day 3 touches this passage) and "Live Like You Belong to Him" (Week 2, Nov 30). Source passage suggested by a Linda Seidler Daily video Lewis shared November 19, 2026 ("Don't let worry have the final word" — Philippians 4:6–7).*

qa.q: How can I be saved?
qa.a: Not by cleaning yourself up first — nobody can. We are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone. Jesus lived the life we could not live and died the death we deserved, and God raises up everyone who trusts Him. Come as you are; leave anchored. There is a page in the Helps — “Plan of Salvation — How to Be Saved” — that walks the whole road verse by verse, bad news first, then the good news.

scriptures.text: because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.

pointers.label: Helps: Plan of Salvation — How to Be Saved
Helps: First Steps for a New Believer

qa.q: How can I know I am really saved?
qa.a: Your assurance does not rest on the strength of your grip on God, but on His grip on you. Feelings come and go; His promise does not. Look at what Christ has done and what God has said, not at how steady you felt this week.

scriptures.text: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

pointers.label: Helps: How Can I Know I'm Really Saved?

qa.q: Can God forgive what I have done?
qa.a: The honest answer starts with the bad news: sin is worse than we like to admit, and God is holy. But the good news is bigger — the blood of Jesus covers the whole record of anyone who confesses and turns. There is no sin confessed at the cross that gets turned away.

scriptures.text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us.

qa.q: I relapsed. Is it over for me?
qa.a: No. A fall is not the end of the story for a man in Christ — it is the place he runs back from, not away. The prodigal was received while he was still far off, rehearsing his speech. Tell the truth, tell somebody today, and come home. His mercies are new every morning, including this one.

scriptures.text: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.

pointers.label: This week's study: Arrest the Thought

qa.q: What do I do when the craving hits?
qa.a: Do not wrestle a craving alone in the dark. God promises a way of escape, and most of the time the way of escape has a phone in it — call somebody, get out of the room, get into the Word. Arrest the thought before it builds a house: take it captive and replace it with what is true.

scriptures.text: No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ.

pointers.label: Study: Arrest the Thought, Fill the Mind

qa.q: How do I pray when I don't know what to say?
qa.a: Prayer is not a performance. Talk to your Father plainly — what hurts, what you need, what you are thankful for. Jesus gave us the pattern: begin with who God is, then bring the day to Him. Short and honest beats long and polished, every time.

scriptures.text: Pray then like this: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.”
Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.

pointers.label: Helps: Where to Find Help in the Bible

qa.q: Why does God feel silent?
qa.a: Silence is not absence. Some of God's most loved people prayed through long quiet seasons — David asked 'how long?' and still called God his rock. Keep opening the Word, keep showing up, and judge God's nearness by His promise, not by the volume of your feelings.

scriptures.text: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?
but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.

qa.q: Why is God letting me suffer?
qa.a: The Bible never hands us a cheap answer, but it hands us a Person. God is not far from suffering — He entered it. The cross proves He can be trusted in the dark, and Romans 8 promises He is working even this for the good of those who love Him. You do not have to understand it to be held in it.

scriptures.text: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.
The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.

qa.q: What does God say about my anxiety?
qa.a: He does not say 'try harder not to care.' He says bring it — all of it, by prayer, with thanksgiving — and His peace will stand guard over your heart and mind like a soldier at the gate. That guard is posted by prayer, and the garrison is Christ Himself.

scriptures.text: do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.

pointers.label: Study: Don't Let Worry Have the Final Word

qa.q: I am afraid. Where do I go?
qa.a: Fear is not a faith failure — it is the weather of a fallen world. David wrote his answer the day the Philistines seized him: when I am afraid, I will trust. Not if — when. The promise is not that nothing scary comes; it is that you will never face it alone.

scriptures.text: When I am afraid, I put my trust in you.
fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand.

qa.q: How do I forgive someone who hurt me?
qa.a: Forgiveness is not saying it did not matter. It is handing the debt to the only Judge who can carry it — and we forgive from the receipt of our own pardon. We were forgiven a debt we could never pay; that is the ground we stand on to release theirs.

scriptures.text: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.

pointers.label: Study: Live Like You Belong to Him

qa.q: What do I do with my anger?
qa.a: Anger itself is not the sin — even Jesus was angry at what sin does to people. The sin comes when anger moves in and starts making decisions. Be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger — and do not let the sun go down on it. Put it off like an old garment; put on kindness instead.

scriptures.text: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.
Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger.

qa.q: I lost someone I love. Does God understand grief?
qa.a: He wept at a grave Himself. Jesus stood at His friend's tomb and cried — knowing resurrection was minutes away. Grief is not weak faith; it is love with nowhere to go, and God draws near to it instead of scolding it. We grieve, but not as those who have no hope.

scriptures.text: Jesus wept.
The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.
But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.

qa.q: My family is broken. Can God restore it?
qa.a: God specializes in putting families back together one changed heart at a time — usually starting with the one asking the question. You cannot control their response, but you can be found faithful: tell the truth, make amends where you can, and let them watch a changed life over time. That witness preaches louder than any argument.

scriptures.text: And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers.
bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.

pointers.label: Study: Live Like You Belong to Him

qa.q: Is it wrong to doubt?
qa.a: Doubt brought honestly to God is not the opposite of faith — Thomas doubted and Jesus met him with His wounds, not a rebuke. What matters is where you take the doubt. Bring it to the Lord and to His people, keep reading, and pray the honest prayer: 'I believe; help my unbelief.'

scriptures.text: Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, “I believe; help my unbelief!”
And have mercy on those who doubt.

qa.q: Do I really need a church?
qa.a: Yes — the Christian life was never designed to be flown solo. We are a body, not an audience: we need the preaching of the Word, the table, and brothers and sisters who will carry us when our own strength runs out. Find a church that opens the Bible and tells the truth with grace, and let people know your name.

scriptures.text: And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.
And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.

qa.q: Where do I start reading the Bible?
qa.a: Start with Jesus. Open the Gospel of John and read a chapter a day, slowly — who is Jesus, what did He do, what does He say to people like me? Then read Romans for the gospel explained. And do not read alone in your head: ask the Lord to teach you before you start, every time.

scriptures.text: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.

qa.q: My thoughts won't stop. How do I take them captive?
qa.a: You cannot stop a thought from knocking, but you do not have to invite it in to live there. Paul's pattern is a trade: arrest the thought — name it, hold it up against God's Word — then fill the mind on purpose with whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, and lovely. Out with the lie, in with the truth, in that order.

scriptures.text: We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ.

Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.

pointers.label: Study: Arrest the Thought, Fill the Mind

qa.q: I am worn out. What does Jesus say to the weary?
qa.a: He says come. Not 'get it together and then come' — come as you are, with the burden still on your back, and He will give you rest. His yoke is easy because He is in it with you, carrying the weight that matters.

scriptures.text: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength.

qa.q: Can God use somebody with my past?
qa.a: Read the family tree of Jesus — it runs through liars, a prostitute, an adulterer, and a murderer. God has always built His story out of people the world counted out. Your past, surrendered, becomes the very place your testimony gets its power: you know exactly what He rescued you from.

scriptures.text: Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.
but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

qa.q: How do I hold on when I want to quit?
qa.a: Some days holding on is all the faith you have — and it is enough, because the holding that saves you is not yours. You are not held up by your grip on God; you are held by His grip on you. Fix your eyes on Jesus, lay the weight down, and take the next step. Then tomorrow, do it again.

scriptures.text: let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith.
And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.

qa.q: Should I be baptized?
qa.a: If you have trusted Christ, yes — baptism is the public sign of the inward reality, the burial of the old life and the rising of the new. It does not save you; it declares Who did. Talk to a local pastor and go public with your faith.

scriptures.text: We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

qa.q: Who is the Holy Spirit, and what does He do in me?
qa.a: The Holy Spirit is God Himself, come to live in everyone who trusts Christ. He convicts us of sin, teaches us from the Word, comforts us in trouble, and grows Christ's character in us — love, joy, peace, and the rest of the fruit — from the inside out.

scriptures.text: But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.

qa.q: How do I tell others about Jesus?
qa.a: Start with your own story — what you were, what happened, what He has done since. Nobody can argue with a changed life they can see. You do not need a seminary degree; you need honesty and love. Tell it when you can, where you can, to anyone you can.

scriptures.text: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect.
Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.

qa.q: What is discipleship?
qa.a: Discipleship is following Jesus daily — learning from Him in His Word and doing what He says, on the ordinary days and not only the strong ones. It costs something real: He asks for all of you, cross and all. But you never walk it alone, and when you stumble you run home, not away — you are held by His grip on you, not your grip on Him. The Helps section walks through the whole thing: what a disciple is, the cost, the daily pattern, and five first steps.

scriptures.text: And he said to all, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me."
So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, "If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples."

qa.q: When you are afraid — where does the Bible meet me?
qa.a: Fear is not a faith failure; it is the weather of a fallen world. But you do not have to live at its mercy.

scriptures.text: When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you.

pointers.label: Open: Where to Find Help in the Bible

qa.q: When you are anxious — where does the Bible meet me?
qa.a: Anxiety is fear pointed at tomorrow. The Lord's answer is not "stop caring" — it is a Person to cast the care on, and a Father who already knows.

scriptures.text: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

pointers.label: Open: Where to Find Help in the Bible

qa.q: When you are grieving — where does the Bible meet me?
qa.a: Grief is love with nowhere to go, and God does not scold it. He draws near to it — and He has wept at a grave Himself.

scriptures.text: The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.

pointers.label: Open: Where to Find Help in the Bible

qa.q: When you are tempted — where does the Bible meet me?
qa.a: Temptation is not sin, and it is not a surprise to God. He has cut an escape route into every single one — the fight is real, and so is the way out.

scriptures.text: No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.

pointers.label: Open: Where to Find Help in the Bible

qa.q: When you are in recovery and fighting craving — where does the Bible meet me?
qa.a: This page was written by a ministry that knows the far country from the inside. The craving is loud, but it is not the loudest voice, and it is not the final one. You are not fighting for God's love; you are fighting from it.

scriptures.text: Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

pointers.label: Open: Where to Find Help in the Bible

qa.q: When you feel far from God — where does the Bible meet me?
qa.a: Feelings are weather; the Word is climate. The distance you feel is real as a feeling — and it is not the measure of where God is.

scriptures.text: Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.”

pointers.label: Open: Where to Find Help in the Bible

qa.q: When you need forgiveness — where does the Bible meet me?
qa.a: Do not clean up first. Do not wait until you feel worthy. The door is confession, and on the other side of it stands a faithful and just God who has already promised what He will do.

scriptures.text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

pointers.label: Open: Where to Find Help in the Bible

qa.q: When you need hope — where does the Bible meet me?
qa.a: Hope in the Bible is not a wish. It is an anchor — something fixed to a rock on the other side of the storm, holding the ship that cannot hold itself.

scriptures.text: It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

pointers.label: Open: Where to Find Help in the Bible

qa.q: How do I become a Christian?
qa.a: You become a Christian the way everyone in the New Testament did: by grace through faith in Jesus Christ — turning from your sin and trusting Him who died and rose for you. It is not joining, earning, or cleaning up first; it is receiving. The Helps page “Plan of Salvation — How to Be Saved” walks it verse by verse.

scriptures.text: that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

qa.q: How do I study the Bible?
qa.a: The same way you eat — a little at a time, in order, and often. Pray first, read the text itself before any notes, watch what it says about God, find Jesus in it, and end with one step to obey and a prayer. This Bible carries the whole road on one page: “How to Study the Bible From A to Z” in the Helps walks all eighteen steps in order, and the SOAP page gives the daily sitting its shape.

scriptures.text: Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.

qa.q: How do I study a passage?
qa.a: Take the passage the A-to-Z way: read it more than once, check its setting, observe what it actually says, keep it in its context, dig into a word or two, follow a cross-reference, find Jesus in it, and land on one step to obey today. The A-to-Z page works one verse — Psalm 46:1 — through the steps, so you can watch it happen before you try it.

scriptures.text: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.

qa.q: How do I share the gospel with someone?
qa.a: Pray for them first, meet them where they are, tell your own story briefly — what you were, what Jesus did, what you are now — then the bad news honestly and the good news fully, and invite a response without pressure. The Helps page “How to Present the Gospel to Someone New” walks the whole conversation in order, Romans Road included.

scriptures.text: For, “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

pointers.label: Helps: How to Present the Gospel to Someone New
Helps: Plan of Salvation — How to Be Saved

qa.q: How do I tell someone about Jesus?
qa.a: Start with your own story — nobody can argue with a changed life they can see. Keep it short and honest: what you were, what He did, what you are now. Then be ready with the gospel itself; “How to Present the Gospel to Someone New” in the Helps gives you the order and the five Romans Road verses to carry in your head.

scriptures.text: But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

qa.q: How do I disciple a new believer?
qa.a: Walk with them the way Jesus walked with His — together, regularly, in the Word. Keep it simple: one passage, one conversation, one prayer at a time, and aim from the first day at the day they disciple somebody else. “How to Disciple Someone New” in the Helps lays out the whole walk, and “Discipleship — Following Jesus Daily” covers the daily pattern underneath it.

scriptures.text: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

qa.q: What do I say when someone asks why God allows suffering?
qa.a: Do not flinch, and do not offer a slogan. We live in a world broken by sin; God has not promised to explain every sorrow, but He did not stay far from ours — in Jesus He entered it, and He will end it. “When They Ask Hard Questions” in the Helps gives you short, honest answers you can actually say out loud — for this question and four more like it.

scriptures.text: For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us.

qa.q: How do I read the Bible with someone else?
qa.a: One-to-one: pick a Gospel — Mark or John — meet weekly at a kitchen table, read a short passage aloud together, and ask three questions: what does it say, what does it mean, what will we do about it. Pray together and keep it under an hour. No prep and no teaching gift required. “Reading the Bible With One Other Person” in the Helps walks it step by step.

scriptures.text: He said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” He begged Philip to come up and sit with him.

qa.q: What is the whole road to salvation?
qa.a: It is one road with every stop in order: God's purpose before time; our start — lost and dead in sin; God drawing us; the gospel heard; the Spirit opening our eyes; repentance and faith; justification; adoption; the daily walk of being made holy; God's grip keeping us to the end; and home. “The Whole Road to Salvation” in the Helps draws the whole map on one page, with Romans 8:29–30 as its spine.

scriptures.text: Whom he predestined, those he also called. Whom he called, those he also justified. Whom he justified, those he also glorified.

pointers.label: Helps: The Whole Road to Salvation

qa.q: How does salvation work from start to finish?
qa.a: From God's side it is one unbroken chain — foreknown, predestined, called, justified, glorified (Romans 8:29–30) — and from our side it is heard, believed, and walked out daily until He brings us home. “The Whole Road to Salvation” in the Helps walks it stop by stop.

scriptures.text: For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.

pointers.label: Helps: The Whole Road to Salvation

qa.q: How does the promise unfold through the whole Bible?
qa.a: Era by era, from Genesis to Revelation: promised in the garden, carried through Noah and Abraham, pictured in the Passover and the sacrifices, promised a kingdom in David, given a face by the prophets, kept in Jesus, preached to the nations by the church, explained in the letters, and arrived home in Revelation. “Salvation Seen Through the Whole Bible” in the Helps traces it mile by mile, with the key verse at each one.
